The great pilgrim of God lost the most immovable and radical asset of the spirit: the hope of finding the truth. Saint Augustine's doubt was not methodical, but distressing and very real in the fight for truth and the spiritual formation of his being. More than a closing of one's eyes to reality, it was the pleading look of a shipwrecked man, a cry of anguish in the infinite desert of brackish waters. Saint Augustine is in the sphere of thought a hero moved by tireless activity in search of light and life. But there was a time in its history when it lost the vigorous belief in the universal dominion of truth. That state was a consequence and result of the ideological crisis in which the failure of Manichaeism plunged him, which had promised to explain things and turned out to be an unsustainable set of unreasons. One by one all his hopes and inner lights went out. The spiritual building, in which he had wanted to take refuge definitively, believing it to be a secure mansion of truth and reason, fell on top of him fragment by fragment, on his aching head, until he was left in the open. This life in the open countryside, without any home of certainty that would give him protection and light until the development of new knowledge, constitutes the academic doubt of Saint Augustine. On the other hand, the immense prestige and oratorical magic of the great Latin orator and one of the perfect stylists of Latin literature intervenes here: Marcus Tullius Cicero. As a professor of rhetoric, Augustine had to rely on the teaching of the Roman orator. At the age of nineteen, Hortensius was the most energetic stimulant to awaken the genius of Saint Augustine and put him on the path of wisdom. One of Cicero's greatest glories is, without a doubt, having fanned the light of the philosophical spirit of the young man from Tagaste, who always kept a pleasant memory of that birth to the love of wisdom. In the schools of his time, Cicero exercised an indisputable teaching, and, together with Virgil, shares the glory of a salutary influence on his spirit. As a philosopher, Cicero is not an original thinker, nor has he contributed great novelties to science; in this sense not

But he was a spirit rich in foreign knowledge, familiar with current literature, both Latin and Greek, and knowledgeable like few others about philosophical doctrines. He had heard the Epicureans, Stoics and Academics discuss, and he corresponded with the most cultured men of his time, who frequented his house: doctissimorwm hominum familiaritates, quibus semper domus riostra floruit5. His teachers were Diodotus, Philo, Antiochus and Posidonius. Antiochus is called polutissimus by the acutissimus omnium noslrae memoriae philosophorum 6. One of Cicero's merits is having given clear and crystalline expression to a great flow of Hellenic thoughts. Saint Augustine himself participated in this heritage and communicated it to the Christian world. But for the topic of our introduction it is worth pointing out here the influence of Cicero on Augustine's academic doubt. The thesis of the Roman philosopher can be summarized in these words: Non sumus ii, quibus nihil verura esse videatur, sed ii qui omnibus veris false quaedam adiuncta esse dicamus tanta similarityine, ut in iis nulla insit certa iudicandi et assentiendi note, ex quo exislit illud, plana esse probabilia, quibus sapientis vita regatur 7. We are not of the who deny the existence of truth at all, but those who maintain that truth and falsehood are so closely linked and mixed that there is no certain sign in them to discern them and give them assent, from which it follows that the wise man must govern his life according to probability. This is the doctrine of the so-called second Academy, which had been introduced into the Roman world by a Greek commission of thinkers, headed by Carneades. In the cited passage from Cicero, the two fundamental attitudes of the academic school stand out: the agnostic speculative attitude, which renounces the knowledge of the truth, because it is veiled with the similarities of the false, and the practical attitude, which relies on the probable, as a standard of conduct. It is the same personal unfolding of the positivist Hipólito Taine: you have to leave the radicalisms of philosophy when you enter the square of life. Nos sequimur probabilia, says the Roman orator. "We follow the probable. The academics said that, to find the probable truth, one must weigh the pros and cons of all opinions: veri inveniendi causa contra omnia dici oportere et pro omnibus *.
That is why very skilled debaters emerged among them,

agile for the fencing of ideas. Philosophical and practical reasons moved Cicero to adhere to the academic school. The oratorical profession required him to manage the discussion, to have dialectical and parliamentary skills. And in the academic school they looked to the formation of the man of agora, to the display of dialectical weapons, to know how to express himself and capture the weak point of human opinions: "For this reason I have always liked the custom of the Peripatetics and the Academy of forming two opposing sides in research, not only because otherwise what is plausible in each thing cannot be reached, but also because it is the best exercise for oratory: sed etiam quod "Esset maxima dicedi exercitalio" ". Naturally, this extreme dialectical habit of discussion gives rise to an agnostic and relativist tendency. As in Manzon's apologist for litigants, everyone is right and no one is right. Everything is true and false according to the color of the glass with which it is viewed. The glass is the subjective and temperamental conditions with which the truth is viewed. But in Cicero one can also see a great reflective effort, a dedicated study of the great themes of Hellenic philosophy, which he incorporated into Latin. Against the vituperators of philosophy, he published in his Hortensius the warm praise of wisdom, which so impressed the young Augustine: nos autem universae philosophiae vituperatoribus responderus in Hortensius." For him, philosophy is the teacher of life: magistra vilae. He was not as radical in his doubt as Pyrrho or Archesilaus himself, since he admits the possibility of a knowledge of the plausible. He deeply pondered the pros and cons of academic probabilism. In the second book of the Academics, which also bears the title of Lucullus, because he is the antagonist and destroyer of academic philosophy, there is a refutation of universal doubt with a series of reasoning that has always opposed sound logic to skepticism. The same reasoning of Saint Augustine in his work Against the Academics gathers the substance of Cicero's opponent. This was what he calls himself: magnus quidem sum opinator 12, and admits the academic principle: Nihil enim arbitrar posse percipi ". Let us strive to show that nothing can be perceived: Nitamur igitur nihil posse percipi." And what are the bases of your proof?

According to Saint Augustine, not only does he err who takes a false path, but also he who does not follow the true one. The apologist of the bivio travelers leads to this conclusion. Systematically suspending judgment, crossing your arms on the bivio or at the innumerable forks in the paths of life, resolves nothing or exempts us from error. Nor is it worth shielding oneself with what is plausible, or an approximation to what is true. CRITERIOLOGICAL VALUE OF THE AXIOMS

With the empirical intuition of psychological experiences, in Augustinian criteria, axioms or principles are favored, captured by a simplex intuitus veritatis, by a simple view of intelligence, which is not only in unbreakable connection with the world of facts or concrete realities, but also with the realm of universal ideas. The intuition of these truths proves the natural capacity to know what is real. They are the movement of truth walking, the astral lamps of knowledge, the anchor of salvation of man's understanding. Here we find a notable difference between the thought of Descartes with his Cogito, ergo sum, and Saint Augustine with the perception of the inner world, much more luminous and richer than that of the French philosopher. Saint Augustine does not intend to found a transcendental science on the basis of the empirical intuition of consciousness, because he knows that there are real truths or existence and ideal truths and canonical laws for the universe. He did not think of deriving the order of truths from the elementary fact of the certainty of consciousness. If the self were the universal support of all essences and existences, the deductive result of this reasoning would be valid. Saint Augustine, then, is far from the romantic thinkers of the 19th century, who were in search of a transcendental science, supported by the intuition of the self. Even Descartes did not succeed in his attempt, because by establishing as a principle the evidence of thought apprehended in its immediacy, he then made the transition to the ideal order, that is, to a universal and necessary idea, admitting as a criterion the clear idea or the necessary relationship and link between thought and existence. For Saint Augustine, humility is the very basis of Christianity and a golden rule in the investigation of truth. To an intellectual who was a little conceited with his literary issues—Dióscoro—he wrote these words, with such resonance and echo in the spirituality of Christianity. The most sublime philosophy of the ancients—Platonic—must pay Christ the homage of its adoration, because He is the Word of God, the exemplary Reason of the universe, clothed in our flesh.

To form, therefore, a deeply truthful and Christian intelligence and to penetrate into the arcana of the real, humility is necessary, because just as sensuality throws man to the exterior, subjecting him to the idolatry of the senses and imagination, so pride closes him in himself, in the narrow mansion of the self, and in both cases it cuts off and diminishes his capacity for flight and the pure freedom of the interior wings. Pride is the steep obstacle that obstructs the entrance to the port of wisdom and a happy life." Also at this point Saint Augustine repeats the lesson of his philosophical experience. Platonism made him puffed up and proud, but it did not reveal to him the difference "between presumption and confession, between those who see where they must go and do not see where and the path that leads to the beatific homeland, which must not only be clear-eyed, but also from within inhabited» ". In concrete terms, Christian humility puts us on the path of Christ, which is the Truth and the Method to reach it. Perhaps this seems a little strange for a criterion, but not for an Augustinian criterion, which is that of the concrete man, called to the highest vocation, which is Christianity. Christ is for Saint Augustine the supreme criterion of absolute Truth, in the ontological, historical and moral sense; the synthesis of wisdom and science, the knowledge of divine and human realities. Christian humility is total adherence to Christ, which illuminates man with double light: eternal and temporal, while being the revelation of the visible and invisible world. In the process of achieving wisdom, according to him, there are three essential milestones: a conquest of. reason by overcoming academic doubt, a conquest of faith by reason and grace and a conquest or intelligence of the contents of faith by wisdom. Faith certainly sharpens reason and even introduces it to the most intimate part of religious truth. This aspect is deeply endearing to Augustinianism. But let us distinguish: first reason prepares for faith, and this then leads to a deeper reason, that is, to the mysterious arcana of the real, manifested by the revelation of Christ. Reason, faith and wisdom summarize the intellectual life in fact and law in Saint Augustine, and this order cannot be altered by saying: faith, reason and wisdom. Reason precedes authority in the historical development of Augustinianism. Father Portalié rightly combats the opinion of Weber *, according to which faith chronologically precedes intelligence; To understand something it is necessary first to embrace it by faith: creedo ut intelligam. But in all these passages, Father Portalié continues, it is only about the intimate understanding of the revealed truths. Here is the radical truth of Augustinian philosophy and existence, the absolute, in which the finite being anchors. This is not the absolute of Aristotle, the pure thought that thinks of itself in a distance. inaccessible; neither the absolute of Neoplatonism, the One to which beings return, to merge in the identity of an eternal substance; nor the absolute of Germanic philosophy, formulated by Hegel and his disciples, or the unknowable of Hartmann, but the living God of the Gospel, immanent in us, intimately linked to our being, without possible rupture, because neither He can leave us nor we can leave Him. The absolute was presented to Saint Augustine after the relativistic and skeptical crisis, as the first and source truth, reason of the cosmos and light of created intelligences. The blessed discovery freed him from academic doubt, providing very deep and new foundations for his existence. His epistemology coincides with this discovery: Intravi in intima mea, duce te, says the great Doctor. Until then he had wandered outside, in the outskirts of truth, in the distant region of the senses, a country of dispersion and hunger.

Then he entered into himself, because the spirit is a prodigious being that has the virtue of entering into itself, into the interior rooms and dwellings. And the most prodigious thing about this interior abode is that it has a zenithal opening, through which the light of the absolute filters. That is, Saint Augustine, entering into himself, discovered the splendor of the being of divinity. The philosophical thought of Saint Augustine involves a double polarity: towards Plato and towards Christ. And note that what must define Christian philosophy as Christian is its polarity towards the second. A philosophy that does not deeply assimilate Christ, what title can it have to call itself Christian? And this connection with Christ is the substance and most formal content of Saint Augustine's philosophical thought. If any philosophy can be called Christian, it is his, due to its radical orientation to explaining everything through the mystery of Christ.

In summary: the conclusion of the books Against the Academics gives us the guidelines of the thought of Saint Augustine, or of Christian philosophy, which contemplates the world in the radiance of the eternal Truth, Christ, in all its connections; It is a Platonic and exemplary philosophy, eminently anthropological, because it studies man in his concrete being, with greater sagacity and depth than any other philosophy. In the fullness of its content it admits the efforts of Aristotle and Plato, who represent the human summit of pure thought. And this not only gives it its own physiognomy, that is, its own content and themes, but also a mentis way, or particular way of looking at the entire world of reality. This is how the philosophy of Saint Augustine was born, which is the flower of Christian philosophy.

In the theory of knowledge they professed a sensualist empiricism, which provoked the second Academy as a reaction. Both Zeno and Chrysippus influenced scholars. Cicero calls this argument lubricum sane et periculosum locum; vitiosum interrogandi genus (Acad, n 28,52). L18] Academic probabilism.—Note that the probabilism of the academic school should not be confused with the probabilism of Catholic moralists, who allow in certain cases to act with a simply probable conscience. The probabilism of the latter does not concern the radical capacity of the understanding to recognize the truth, but refers to the solution of certain practical cases of uncertainty of a law, in which it is legal to favor freedom, based on solid reason. The system of Catholic morality is based on the certainty of many laws of natural and positive order that regulate the acts of conscience for the most part. Probabilists demand that for a law to be mandatory it must be true, and this is a reason contradictory to the academic principle. I. When Augustine converted, first to Platonism and then to Christianity, he had to say a sincere and eternal goodbye to Manichaeism, whose doctrines, in the light of the new truths, already appeared as a motley set of absurdities and meaningless nonsense. But it was not in vain that they had made a nest in his chest for nine years in a row, the sweetest and most flowery of his youth. The glass that has long had an intense liquor or perfume, writes the Mantuan poet (and the Saint conveniently remembers on another occasion on the occasion of his classical readings), even after emptying and washing, retains the persistent smell of its first essence. Augustine had well filled the glass of his intelligence with the deleterious doctrines of Manichaeism; What was strange that, attached to them for so many years with sincerity and sympathy, they left in his soul the pungent odor of their memory and the persistent aftertaste of their first acquiescence? 'If the skepticism of the new Academy, although it had been sporadic and fleeting in him, left in his soul a strong yeast of pessimism and distrust, which he later found himself forced to combat through serious meditations and disputes with his friends and disciples, in order to uproot it and expel it from him completely, thereby purging his conscience again and again, in his graphic expression,' how much would they leave behind doctrines so joyfully received, so flattering to the senses and passions and so simplistic in their moral and metaphysical solutions? This is, without a doubt, the reason why, as soon as he leaves his professorship and retires to Casicíaco, he dedicates himself fully and with all the ardor of his African temperament to the work of interior cleansing and clearing, to a true and profound intellectual catharsis, reviewing piece by piece the entire mechanism of his inner life, to ascertain the resistance and value of each one and the security of the conquered ground. And this is also why all of the Saint's works from this first period of his intellectual activity are eminently apologetic and combative, except for the precious literary toy De magistro and the six books On music, also written somewhat late, despite the fact that almost all of them, or at least many of them, take on the character of mere school exercises or philosophical essays.

The conquest, however, of the truth; The sincere surrender of an intelligence certainly does not imply full and total control of it, nor does it imply that there is no dark and difficult point left in the deepest recesses. Augustine had been conquered by the truth, but there were still remnants of his past in the mysterious depths of his conscience; There were still dark and difficult points that he wanted to clarify at all costs and as soon as possible. Agustín feels the need to recover completely and to recover his friends for the truth, achieved with so much work and fatigue. His ideal is no longer other than his own conquest and that of others. All his writings and speeches are inspired by this double feeling, and through it they must be read and studied. Although Manichaeism included a complicated series of errors and delusions of a religious, physical and moral order, we must recognize that in all of them the principle or theory of the existence of evil beats and stirs: metaphysical evil and moral evil. Augustine believed in many other Manichaean absurdities, as he himself tells us in his Confessions; but none penetrated so deeply into his heart as this one. And we all have the problem of good and evil posed with compelling characters in the depths of our soul, and when a materialist solution has been nailed to it, it is not easy to remove it except with another nail in the opposite direction. Augustine would hardly have been able to get rid of it if Platonism had not come to shed intense light on his intelligence and demonstrate with all evidence that evil is not a real being existing by itself, but rather a lack of good, a deprivation of being due, a defect of natural integrity. Like a house of cards, the immense Manichean ontological contraption collapsed in one moment, a! first contact of the very vivid light that Platonic philosophy shed at this point. But, on the other hand, moral evil, the existence of sin, the ultimate reason for its existence, did not seem so easy to understand and explain. Augustine, always logical with himself and accustomed to seeing problems and the world through the latest system he embraced, understood that if before he had given all the solutions according to the Manichean prism, he must now give them according to the new doctrines professed, and which he believed to be inconclusive, although he did not understand many of their conclusions.

He saw clearly that sin consisted substantially of something negative, but he was not yet able to fully understand that negativity and even less so the reason for its existence, without somehow complicating the providence and action of God. Both things worried his intelligence and he wanted to give them full clarification, for his inner satisfaction and for the response and instruction of his friends in Manichaeism, who, well accommodated with the solutions,

However, this consideration troubles our spirit: If sin comes from the souls that God created, and souls come from God, how can we not refer sin to God, the relationship between God and the sinful soul being so close? Words to which Evodio puts this culmination: "You have just formulated with complete clarity and precision the doubt that cruelly torments my heart and what has brought us to this discussion in which we are engaged." The issue really could not be spoken or posed with greater clarity and precision. But how can we fully understand the origin of sin without first knowing its essence? And what does sin consist of? Augustine does not define this until the end of the first book, trying first to find out what the source and cause of it is, what the reasons why the soul sins, what role the passions, reason, law, eternal and temporal, play in it, to reach this final conclusion: man, like every being, is subject to an eternal and immutable law, which he must not transgress; However, harassed by the appetite for goods or pleasures, prohibited by that same law, man sometimes abandons this law to follow the former. However, there is nothing that can fatally force man and his free will to obey the passions; These can tempt you, seduce you, force you, but not irresistibly force you to follow and obey them. Concupiscence is the occasion to sin, but not the cause of sin, which lies in free will.

Therefore free will is an evil for man, exclaims Evodio. Wouldn't it be better to lack such a sad prerogative? The second book is occupied almost entirely by the so-called proof of the existence of God, in which Augustine explains his theory of knowledge, starting from the sensitive and animal knowledge to the purely intellectual and abstract. Under this aspect, these chapters have a very unique interest for Augustinian noetics. In them, the ascension method of the Saint is also advocated: from external objects to the senses, from the external senses to the internal ones, from the internal senses to reason, from reason to the eternal and immutable truths* or intelligible world, and from the intelligible world to God. God is claimed by the existence of the intelligible world, which we cannot doubt. Augustine arrives through a series of reasonings at the concept of God as an essentially good, totally good and infinitely good being, from whom all being and all goodness comes. Therefore, everything that is good in the world necessarily comes from God, and will be all the more good the more it participates in his goodness; Therefore the evil of the creature is in the least participation or in the due lack of such goodness. Agustín goes one step further. Free will is in itself a good, not an evil (c. x v m ff.). Then he explains how the abuse of a good does not imply that that good becomes evil. The eyes, arms, tongue, etc., although they become instruments of evil for man and are used in bad things, do not cease to be a good in themselves, why should free will be? We all love freedom, we all want freedom, we all long for freedom, as a sovereign good, as the greatest good that man can enjoy on earth; And if we consider only the loss of external, material freedom as an immense evil, what could it not be that which concerns the will itself, and which we call free will? If evil lay in the essence of free will, there would be reason to blame God; But being in itself a good, its evil can only be in a defect of itself, in a weakness of the will, letting oneself go after a sensible good, a delight, postponing the supreme good, God. In essence, all this is nothing more than an application of Plato's theory of good and evil. Saint Augustine distinguishes or divides goods into three classes: great, medium and minimum.

«Great, the goods that are always great and can never be evils, like the virtues; means, those that can sometimes serve evil, such as the powers of the soul, and minimums, earthly goods, such as beauty, vigor of the body, agility, etc. Free will is a medium good, because we can use it badly; However, it is such that without it we cannot act well and laudably. Si quid aulem de origine peccati diligentius quaerendum adhuc putas, nam omnino ego iam opus esse non arbitror, ​​si quid tamen putas, in aliam disputationem differendum est. It was not easy for Evodio's discontented spirit to be satisfied with what had been said, so he gladly postponed the dispute for a better occasion, in exchange for giving it a satisfactory end in all its parts. The third book is, therefore, a complement and, in many of its chapters, a clarification of the previous one. In the introduction he feels again that the guilty movement of the will, by which it separates itself from God, comes solely from free will, and that its power to sin arises from its weakness to do good. He then tries extensively to harmonize free will with the foreknowledge of God. Man does not sin, says the Saint, because God has foreseen it. Everything that God foresees will necessarily happen, because God is infallible; But God sees things as they are in themselves, the free as free and the necessary as necessary, since each thing must act according to its nature. God sees sin before man commits it, because, knowing all future things, God cannot ignore the actions of his creatures. But God cannot foresee the necessity of an intrinsically free action, without a manifest contradiction. The existence of a thing is totally different from its being or essence; existence can be necessary, without its being being.

Or in other words: everything that God has foreseen to exist, will exist infallibly, necessarily, because the science of God cannot be deceived or fail; but it will exist according to its way of being, free or necessary. If I were a prophet, future things would not happen because I foresaw them, but I would foresaw them because they were to exist. But if sin is a lack of being, where does God see it? IV. Saint Augustine proceeds in this work as a Christian philosopher rather than as a theologian. It is nothing strange that it has its weaknesses, and sometimes even imprecise ones, as the Saint recognizes. The Pelagians tried to rely on some chapters and phrases of this work to defend their errors'; but in vain, because although the Saint, when he wrote it, could not keep in mind such errors, which had not yet arisen, the inaccuracies of some chapters are corrected with the very clear doctrine of others. In fact, if they had read the work slowly, they would have seen later that the author does not attribute to free will an all-embracing power to do good or evil, regardless of the current state of sin and decay of nature as a result of the first transgression and an endless series of moral diseases transmitted by inheritance. Augustine accuses the existence of a first sin of nature, and this was enough so that the Pelagians could not in any way allege this book in their favor. It is true that he does not speak insistently about grace, as medicine and help for free will, but he hints at it several times, and one of them expressly. What the Saint repeats a thousand times is that man is free to do good and that he is not bound to do evil by any necessity. If man sins, it is his fault. If God punishes him for it, it is a sign that he was free when committing it. Saint Augustine insists unceasingly on the essential and infinite goodness of God, in whom there is nothing but goodness, and from whom nothing but good things can come; He is a loving father, who even when punishing shows himself to be good; If he has given us free will it is because it is a great good; so great good that man prefers to lose everything before Saint Augustine points out the numbers and chapters that these alleged: De libero arbitrio 1.1: 1,1; 12.26; 13,28-29; 14:30, and 16:34; 1.2: 1.2; 17.47; 1.3: 1.2; 3.7; 16.46; 18.49-50.

God THE AUTHOR OF EVIL?

1. Evodio.— -Tell me, I beg you: can God be the author of evil? Agustín.—I'll tell you, if you first tell me what evil you mean, because there are two meanings that we usually give to the word evil: one, when we say that "someone has done evil"; another, when we affirm that "someone has suffered some evil." Ev.—Of both, I wish to know who the author is. Ag.—God being good, as you know or believe—and it is certainly not licit to believe otherwise—it is clear that he cannot do evil. Furthermore, if we confess that God is just—and denying it would be blasphemy—just as he rewards the good, he also punishes the bad; and there is no doubt that the pains with which he afflicts them are an evil for them. Now, if no one who suffers suffers unjustly, as we are forced to confess, since we believe in divine Providence, regulating everything that happens in the world, it follows that God is in no way the author of the first type of evil, but of the second. Ev.—Is there, then, another author of that first kind of evil, of which we have just seen that God is not the author?

And, finally, the law that has been given for the defense of the people cannot be argued to be passionate; because if the one who gave it did so by order of God, that is, in accordance with the principles of eternal justice, he could do so absolutely free from all passion, and if he did it moved by some passion, it does not follow from this that this law must be obeyed passionately, since a bad legislator can give good laws. If a tyrant of usurpation, for example, receives from a citizen, who is interested, a sum of money so that he can decree that no one is allowed to kidnap a woman, not even to marry her, will this law be bad because it was given by that unjust and corrupt tyrant? One can, therefore, fulfill without passion the law that commands the repelling of force.

30. Aug.—Perfectly. But do you think there is any man who does not want and does not long above all to live a happy life? Ev.—Who doubts that every man wants it? But now I don't know what contradiction appears, which, if we do not examine and undo it thoroughly, could ruin our previous conclusions, so scrupulous and firmly established. How do you explain that those who live a miserable life do so of their own free will, when no one wants to live miserably? Or how can we explain that by his own will man manages to live a happy life, when there are many miserable people, despite the fact that everyone wants to be happy? Perhaps this will happen because it is one thing to want to live well or badly, and quite another to deserve something by virtue of good or bad will. In fact, those who are happy—and to be so they must also be good—are not so precisely because they have wanted to live a happy life, for this is what the bad people also want, but because they have wanted to live well or rightly, something that the bad people do not want. Ag.—The Lord will grant me, as I hope, to be able to answer you, or rather, for you to answer yourself, illuminated internally by that truth that is the sovereign and universal teacher of all. Even more so; Everyone who reflects on the true notion of unity sees that it cannot be perceived by the senses of the body. In fact, what our senses perceive, whatever it may be, is not constituted by unity, but by plurality; because, being by necessity a body, it therefore consists of countable parts. And, even leaving aside the smallest and least articulated parts of any body, no matter how minimal it may be assumed, it undoubtedly has a right and a left part, an upper and a lower, or an anterior and a posterior, or an extreme and a middle. We cannot help but confess that all this is found in every body, no matter how tiny it may be; We cannot grant, therefore, that there is any body that is a true unity, and yet we could not enumerate in it such an infinity of distinct parts except through the concept of unity. By searching for unity in the body and being sure of not finding it, I know certainly what it is that I am looking for there, what it is that I do not find there and cannot find it, or rather,

nor can it be found there. If, then, I know that the body is not a unity, I know what unity is, since, if I did not know what unity is, I could not distinguish many and diverse parts in the same body. But wherever I see unity, I certainly will not see it through the senses of the body, because through the senses we know only bodies, and true and pure unity, we are convinced that it is not a body. Finally, if we do not perceive the unity through the senses of the body, we do not perceive through them any number, of those, I say, that we intuit through intelligence, because there is none of them that does not take its name from the number of times it contains the unity, whose intuition does not take place through the senses of the body. And continuing like this through the entire series of the remaining numbers, you will find in all the numbers what you have verified in the sum of the first ones, in one and in two; You will see that any number consists of as many units, counting from the first inclusive, as many as there are between it and its double. Now, by what intimate faculty do we perceive the immobility, firmness and unalterability of this law, which we see fulfilled in the entire series of numbers? No man can encompass all the numbers with the senses of the body, since they are innumerable. How, then, do we come to know this law, which chains everyone, or through what fantasy or what image do we see this truth so certain of numbers, and with such unbreakable firmness through the indefinite series of them, but with the inner light, ignored by the bodily senses? 24. These and many other proofs of this genus obliduplum eius habet; duo enim sequuntur. Post tertium, id est ternarium, ipso except tertius sit qui duplus est eius: post tertium enim, id est post ternarium primus est quaternarius, secundus quinarius, tertius senarius, qui duplus est tertii. Atque ita post quartum. ipso except quartus habet duplum eius: post quartum enim. id est quaternarium, primus est quinarius, secundus senarius, tertius septenarius, quartus octonarius, qui duplex est quarti.

Ev.—I do not know what wisdom you speak of, because I see that the opinion of men differs greatly regarding wisdom, or when pointing out what the work consists of or speaking wisely: for it seems to those who follow the military that they act wisely; Those who despise military art, to put all their effort and work into the cultivation of the fields, preferentially praise this occupation and attribute wisdom to it; To those who are skilled in excogitating means of earning money, it seems to them that they are wise; Those who despise and give away all these things and all those that are temporal, and give themselves fully to the investigation of the truth to know themselves and know God, consider this to be the greatest and noblest occupation and proper to wisdom; Those who do not want to devote themselves to the search and contemplation of the truth, but to the cares and duties, the most painful, in order to be useful to Humanity, and are concerned with the just direction and government of human affairs, consider themselves to be wise; and to those who do one thing or another, and part of their life is dedicated to the contemplation of the truth, part to the works of service, which they believe human society owes, it seems to them that they are the ones who hold the palm of wisdom. I omit innumerable sects, of which there is not one that, putting its followers before the others, does not want to vindicate for itself the name of wise men.

Therefore, when it comes to us now, the answer is not what we believe, but what is it that we clearly see and have sapientias? an vero unam praesto esse communiter omnibus, cuius quanto magis quisque fit particeps, mucho est sapientior? Because of our intelligence, I cannot in any way answer what you have asked before contemplating and also expressing by reason what I know by faith, that is, what wisdom itself consists of. 26. Ag.—Do you think that there is another wisdom other than the truth, in which the highest good is contemplated and possessed? All these men whom you have summoned and who pursue are diverse objects, they all desire good and flee from evil, and if they strive for such diverse things, it is because each one has a different concept of good. And so, he who desires what he should not desire is wrong, although he would not really desire it if it did not seem good to him. Only he who desires nothing or he who desires what he must desire cannot make a mistake. Therefore, inasmuch as all men desire the blessed life, they do not and err. The error of each person is that, confessing and proclaiming that they wish nothing more than for happiness to come, they nevertheless do not follow the path of life that leads to it. The error is, then, that, following a path, we follow one that does not lead to where we want to get. And the more one errs on the path of life, the less one knows; because it is so much more distant from the truth, in whose contemplation and possession consists the highest good. And blessed is the man who has come to know and possess the highest good, which we all desire without any doubt. If, then, it is clear that we all want to be blessed, it is equally clear that we all want to be wise, because no one who is not wise is blessed, and no one is blessed without the possession of the supreme good, which consists of knowledge ad id tibi quod interrogasti I will answer potero, nisi quod credendo teneo. contemplating etiam et ratione cernendo noverim, quae sit ipsa sapientia. 26.

Aug.—Num aliam putas esse sapientiam nisi veritatem, in qua cernitur et tenetur summum bonum? And it is clear that from this multitude of things each one voluntarily chooses those that he wishes to enjoy: through the sense of sight, one enjoys seeing and contemplating the height of some mountain, another the plain of the countryside, this one the depth of the valleys, that one the greenery of the forests, that one the uniform movements of the waters of the sea, and, finally, the one from beyond enjoys seeing and contemplating, as much as he can, all these things. together or some of them.

4. This being so, I am, however, extremely worried, because I cannot understand how it can be that God knows all futures in advance and that, nevertheless, we do not sin out of necessity. Therefore, if God foresaw that the first man would sin, which cannot but be granted by anyone who believes with me that God has foreknowledge of all futures, if this is so, as there can be no doubt, I do not therefore say that God should not have created man, since he created him good, and the sin of man, whom he himself created in all his goodness, can in no way be opposed to the action of God; even more: in which he showed his goodness in creating it, his justice in punishing it, and his mercy in redeeming it. Since it is impossible not to will, those who want a thing have a will, and yet nothing is in their power except what they have, when they want to have it. Our will, therefore, would not be ours if it were not in our power, and because it is in our power, that is why it is free, since it is clear that what is not free is not in our power or that, being free, can cease to be free. THE VERY CORRUPTION OF THE CREATURE AND THE VITUPERATION OF HIS VICES MANIFEST HIS GOODNESS

Every creature that can be less good is good, and every creature, when it is corrupted, loses its goodness, because either it is not affected by corruption, and in this case it is not corrupted, or, if it is corrupted, it is affected by corruption, and if it is affected, it diminishes its goodness and makes it less good. If corruption deprives it of all good, it can no longer be corrupted, since it has no good left that could give rise to corruption. That which cannot be affected by corruption and nature that is not corrupted is incorruptible. There would, then, be a creature made incorruptible through corruption, which would be a major absurdity. Therefore it is very rightly said that all nature, in so far as it is nature, is good; because, if it is incorruptible, it is better than the corruptible, and if it is corruptible, it is, without a doubt, good, since by being corrupted it becomes less good. Now every nature is either corruptible or incorruptible: therefore every nature is good. I understand by nature what we usually give the name of substance. Therefore every substance is either God or comes from God, because all good is either God or comes from God. 37. 29. Ag.—Depose your admiration, because I will now put a similar argument to the contrary. man is a mortal animal, it is equally true: every mortal animal is a man. Quamobrem ista nostra definitio suscepta tua, non solum alienes invasisse terms, ñeque aliquid sui iuris reliquisse, sed nihil omnino habuisse proprium, totumque alienum occupasse convicta est. Et ego quidem tametsi obtinere non potui, bona fide adfui, quod mihi satis est: tu vero si praevaricationis arguaris, quid facías, a quo et producta est ut iurgaret audenter, et oppugnata ut turpiter cedeet? Ag.—Well, although sensation is one thing and science another, nevertheless, not hiding things in both cases is common to both; in the same way that being an animal is common to man and beast, although they differ greatly from each other. Ev.—I am very impressed by this conclusion. So much so that I am completely stupefied, and not only can I not find what to answer, but I don't know, at all, where I am. What shall I say then? What is it not a sensation when the passion of the body does not hide itself from the soul? What else will it be if not this? That the eyes suffer nothing when we see? This is completely absurd. That the eyes suffer where they are? But they do not see themselves, nor is there anything more than them where they are. That the soul is not more powerful than the eyes, being itself their power? I cannot in any way persuade myself that this movement is carried out without a soul, nor do I understand how it can be that the soul has no spatial extension, when it can also be divided with the body. Ag.—I could answer that the air and fire, which are preserved in the earthly and humid body by the presence of the soul so that the harmony of the four elements exists, while, after the separation of the soul, they go out to the higher regions and get rid of themselves, move those little bodies all the more quickly the more quickly they come out through the recent wound; then, afterward, the movement languishes and dies, finally, as what escapes becomes smaller, and finally it all disappears. But what I saw with these eyes separates me from this conception, almost later than one might think, but, in truth, not later than it should be. While recently in the countryside in Liguria, those of our young people who were with me at the time due to their studies, lying on the ground in the shade, observed a small animal with many feet that was crawling, that is, a long worm. It is known to everyone, but what I will say now I had never experienced in him. One of those young men, who happened to have a style, turned to divide the animal in half. Then the two parties, starting from the wound on the body, marched in the opposite direction with such speed and with such impetus as if they were two different animals. Surprised by that prodigy and eager to know the cause, they happily brought us those pores; quem motum sine anima fieri nullo moda mihi persuadere possum: ñeque quo pact fiat, ut nullum sit animae spatium, quando praecidi etiam cum corpore potest, intelligo. Aug.—Possem will respond aerem et ignem, quae duo per animae praesentiam tenentur in corpore terrain et humido, ut omnium quatuor fiat contemperado, dum post eiusdem abscessum ad superna evadunt, ac sese expediunt, moveré illa corpuscula tanta concitatius, quanto piaga recentiore súbito erumpunt: deinde porro motum languescere, desserto desinere, dum minus minusque fit quod effugit, ac deinde totum evolat. Sed ab hoc me revoke quod his hausi oculis penis serius quam credi potest; sed certe non serius quam debenem.

Cum enim nuper in agro essemus Liguriae, nostri illi adulescentes qui tune mecum erant studiorum suorum gratia, animadverterunt humi iacentes in opaque loco, reptantem bestiolam multipedem, longum dico quemdam vermiculum: vulgo no tus est, hoc tamen quod dicam nunquam in eo expertus eram. Verso namque stilo quem forte habebat unus illorum, animal medium percussit: tum ambae partes corporis ab illo vulnere incontra discesserunt, tanta pedum celeritate, ac nihilo imbecilliore nisu, quam si duo huiuscemodi animantia forent. Quo miraculo exterriti, causaeque curiosi, ad nos, ubi simul ego et Alypius considebamus, ala-i Trigetius and Licentius, son of Romanianus.

VERSION, INTRODUCTION AND NOTES
P. MANUEL MARTÍNEZ, O. S. A.

1. The precious philosophical dialogue The Master was written in 389. Augustine, after having received baptism in Milan from the hands of Saint Ambrose (387) and staying for some time in Rome, went to Africa. His soul was saturated with the monastic idealism that he had admired in Milan and Rome, as he himself teaches us in his work De moribus Ecclesiae catholicae1. After his arrival in Tagaste, his small homeland, he distributed all his assets in alms, keeping only the usufruct of his paternal house, where he retired with some friends, founding there the first African monastery. Time was divided between exercises of piety, manual work and study. Augustine applies himself preferentially to the study of holy Scripture and the composition of apologetic works. 2. Among the first monks of Tagaste lived the one whom Augustine humbly calls "the son of his sin" ~, the young Adeodatos, who is the interlocutor of the dialogue The Master. He was sixteen years old, and the author of the Confessions assures that all the thoughts put on his lips are his. It is surprising that, at that tender age, Adeodato manifested that admirable ingenuity. 3. The dialogue The Master seems to indicate that Augustine continued Adeodato's literary education in Tagaste. The conversation begins with the serious issue of the reason for language. Afterwards, Augustine chooses a verse from Virgil as an example, and the discussion develops at length about the grammatical role of the first words. One question raises another, without rigorous logical order, but not without subtlety; Augustine asks his disciple to summarize the points examined. Having done this, the teacher seems to have scruples: he remembers, perhaps, that he is a monk; He excuses himself from indulging in these literary games and promises to lead Adeodatus to a very high moral doctrine, "to the country of the blessed life." 4. But this will not be the shortest way. Once again the discussion begins again on the various kinds of signs and on the value of language as a sign of things. Soon, however, Augustine's goal becomes clearer: "Is it truly impossible," he asks, "to teach anything without words and without sensible signs?" And through a series of clever questions and very typical examples, he demonstrates the radical impotence of language to convey the truth.

5. There is nothing left but to indicate the true Master. He does so in a continuous speech, which fills the third part of the work. This Master is Christ, who is the same truth that dwells in the most intimate part of our souls. The human teacher is content to invite the disciple to turn towards the inner truth, to allow himself to be illuminated by its radiance; because, according to the word of Jesus, "we have only one teacher, Christ" \ 6. The interest of this dialogue lies not so much in the logical and grammatical discussions as in the important doctrine of enlightenment, clearly taught here by Saint Augustine for the first time. In the De beata vita, written in 386 in Casiciaco, it is found as a presentiment in the identification of wisdom, the principle of the blessed life, with the truth and with Christ, who said: "I am the truth" (n.34). But the Master makes it entirely explicit and gives us one of the most vigorous demonstrations. 7. Jolivet has said, very correctly, that the doctrine of illumination occupies the center of Augustinianism 4. She always exercised the sagacity of researchers, and did not frequently find them in agreement. The purpose of this book is not to settle the controversies, but to provide an important piece of the process to researchers eager to form an opinion for themselves. 8. It is necessary to keep in mind that in Saint Augustine - the synthetic and concrete method being the basis, everything oriented towards the moral and religious instruction of the reader - the exact meaning of a philosophical statement cannot be understood without keeping in mind the entire system. Thus the author of The Master exposes a doctrine, above all psychological, when studying our knowledge of the truth; but it also leads to piety, by recommending docility to Christ-Truth; and even more to metaphysics, by outlining his preferred way or means to demonstrate the existence of God. 9. From this last point of view, the two Augustinian works The Master and Free Will have a certain relationship. The first outlines the general picture of the proof by the theory of illumination; It assumes God present within the soul rather than demonstrates it. The second, in her second book, exposes in all its breadth the march of reason towards God. 10. We will still point out the theory of memory, which makes important progress in The Master, before expanding on the enthusiastic descriptions of the Confessions and the profound analyzes of the De Trinitate °.

We now want to broadly explain some points of doctrine that will help us better understand this beautiful and original work of Saint Augustine. 13. Theory of reminiscence.—To explain the first principles, foundations of science (what Saint Augustine called eternal truths), several philosophers admit that the soul possesses them from its union to the body and that it preserves them unconsciously, in a kind of memory, until the warning or warning of reason; In this way, he does not receive them from experience or teaching, he remembers them. Such is the theory of reminiscence, which appears in history under three main forms. The first recognizes Plato (429-348 BC) as its author, and is followed by his Neoplatonic disciples, particularly Plotinus (205-270 AD) and Porphyry (232-305). The soul, supposedly pre-existing, acquired the sciences in its previous life; Later locked in a body as punishment for some fault, she forgot everything due to her union with matter; Thus the study of science in this life is, in its own sense, a memory. Saint Augustine, versed in the works of Plotinus and Porphyry, knew this theory from the beginning of his Catholic life, although he seems to have never admitted it.

It was contradicted by Holy Scripture, either by Genesis (2, 7), recounting the creation of the soul of the first man, or by Saint Paul, "teaching that before being born no one has done works, neither good nor bad; on the other hand, we know that in the days of his conversion he read Saint Paul, in preference to the Platonic books. The second form is innatism. God, by creating the soul

Theory of illumination.—The acquisition of wisdom must be explained, according to Saint Augustine, by the illumination of divine truth, that is, by a richer creative influence, which makes our soul participate not only in temporal and spatial perfections (substantial being, vegetative life, animal knowledge), which are still subject to change, but also in its immutable perfection. truth. The dialectical process most familiar to the Saint is to ascend to God as the light of the created spirits, reflected in the eternal truths. Augustinian philosophy is a song in the light of the uncreated Truth, subsisting by itself. All created lights must be lit in their primordial source, they need it to shine. Human reason, as light, has the same condition; justice.

Since 387, in the Soliloquies ", Saint Augustine had called God the sun of spirits, whose role was to make intelligible objects understood; but he gave this idea as a probability; in The Master he teaches it for the first time as true; Towards this same time, he also exposed it in

In this theory two aspects must be distinguished: the fact and the mode of illumination. There is no discussion about the first; Regarding the second, they are all discussions. Among the proposed interpretations, it is necessary to discard the pantheistic one, which assumes that we are only passive, as if God only worked in us through illumination; Saint Augustine frequently points out that we have an intelligence different from God. We must also reject the ontological interpretation, which explains the characteristics of necessity, immutability and eternity of our sciences, giving as the immediate object of our intelligence the divine ideas that have precisely those qualities, and in which we know all things. Ontologism assumes that we see all things in God. Saint Augustine, whose intuitive method seems to ignore the distinction between God and his created image, more than once uses expressions that insinuate, in effect, vision in God 16. But other very explicit Augustinian texts are incompatible with ontologism. Malebranche certainly departs from Saint Augustine when he says that we see in God all truth, even regarding sensible things. The holy Doctor denies to our intelligence, in the natural order, the power to see God directly; He only grants this power on rare occasions in the mystical life, for example, to explain the ecstasies of Moses and Saint Paul 17; while enlightenment is a common benefit, received by every spirit as soon as it attains the truth. Anyway, in Contra Faust. ", Saint Augustine clearly distinguishes the uncreated light of the Word from another light where the object of wisdom appears to us. Here, to understand Saint Augustine's expressions well, it is necessary to place ourselves in his point of view, which is that of Platonic participation. Our life and our being come whole at every moment from God, and in this sense "we live and exist in God"; in the same way, our knowledge of the truth comes from God, and in this sense "we see the truth in God." "These Augustinian forms—says Gilson—express nothing more than the total ontological dependence of human understanding in relation to God, from whom it has being, activity and life. Such is the true meaning of this immediate contact of our intelligence with information.

Saint Thomas, seeking the truth more than the historical thought of the authors, shows the agreement of Augustinian doctrine with his own theories of abstraction and the divine notion: God, in effect, is the light of the soul, as a source in which our intelligence participates, and in particular our agent understanding, whose function is to illuminate the sensible object (contained in the phantasm) to make it intelligible in action. At the end of his introduction to Aristotle's logic, Porphyry asks: What do universal ideas mean?

salts? Are they subsistent realities or simple notions of intelligence? Roscelin (around 1050-1120) responded: «Universals are words, noises of the voice; because only individuals are realities; "words that apply to several individuals are therefore not things." He thus reduces universals to what Saint Augustine calls verba, words that hurt the ear. Abelard (1079-1142) is not satisfied with this superficial answer. According to him, the universe is not a vox (Roscelin), but a sermo or nomen, that is, what has the ability to be predicated of many, that is, a conception of our spirit, but without correspondence to any reality (conceptualism). Abelard's nominalism agrees with the Augustinian etymology of nomen; but it is not certain that he was inspired by The Master, although the philosophical works of Saint Augustine were known and appreciated in his time. Abelard rather follows Boethius and Aristotle, and insists on the logical function of nomen, which, according to him, "is capable of being predicated of several subjects in a judgment"; From this point of view, the universal nomen is not a thing. Finally, continuing his investigations in the psychological order, Abelard sees in the thing signified by the name nature itself, which the individual realizes in a concrete way, and which the spirit considers in its state of abstraction. St. Augustine has quite different concerns; If he examines signs, and especially words and their relationships with the things signified, it is to demonstrate the secondary role of signs, words and names, in order to direct the spirit towards the inner Teacher, whose teaching alone can make us understand the things signified. 16. Faith and science.—Saint Augustine seeks to demonstrate in The Master that true intellectual knowledge, the science or intelligence of things, is only possible to us through the teaching of the inner Master, Christ. The words, which warn us from outside, coming from a human teacher, can at most engender belief in us. How should we understand these two acts: believing and knowing? The holy Doctor uses terminology that is not perfectly clear. Firstly, it does not explicitly distinguish between natural faith and supernatural faith.

In The Master it seems primarily about human faith, founded on the authority of creatures; because the discussion that fills the first part moves on the natural plane, and if the words of a verse of Virgil or the teaching of an Epicurean master can engender a belief, it is a purely human belief. But it is also about supernatural faith, founded on the authority of God, which reveals to us the truths necessary for eternal life; because Saint Augustine relies preferably on sacred authors and revealed books; Thus, he says, quoting St.

Paul: «Well, to resort to the authority that is most dear to us...» (n.14); He takes the typical example of the saraballas from the prophet Daniel, and in the fundamental text: "Ñisi credideritis, non intelligetis", it is about supernatural faith in divine teachings. The same synthetic method is found in the other works where Saint Augustine addresses the question. Thus, in De utilitate credendi (written around the year 391, with the aim of converting his friend Honorato, a Manichean), to demonstrate the need to begin with faith, he invokes two facts of human belief. Children do not know that their parents are truly theirs; because they do not believe in their fathers except through the authority of their mothers, and they do not believe in their mothers except through the authority of servants and nurses. On the other hand, the purpose of the work is also to show the true method of salvation, and, consequently, it is also about supernatural faith, which must precede the science of the things of God, contrary to the method of the Manichaeans. Saint Augustine grants this supernatural purpose a central and preponderant place in all his works; He constantly tries to get closer to him and lead the others there. The Master makes no exception to this rule, despite grammatical discussions. In chapter vni, 21, the Holy Father clearly implies it: the happy life to which he wants to lead Adeodato is the perfect Christian life, and, finally, heaven. This is why, if one wants to understand the Augustinian formula fully wherever faith and science are concerned, it is necessary to think about supernatural faith. And this faith is not an entirely speculative belief, but a faith vivified by charity, a total adherence that subjects intelligence and the entire life to divine authority, so that the soul finds its purification there and is willing to receive the teaching and illumination of Christ, which brings it science and intelligence: "Intellectus enim est “merces fidei” 2S. On the other hand, the most perfect knowledge that enriches the initial faith, and which the Master calls science or intelligence, is usually called wisdom. But between these three terms, Saint Augustine establishes the precise nuances. Thus, in De Trinitate he distinguishes and even opposes science and wisdom.

Science is the work of lower reason, which considers things from the temporal and human point of view; This is why, considered in isolation, it easily unites itself with creatures to enjoy them as an end, thus being the origin of greed, the root of all evils, and inciting pride, the first of all sins. Such a science does not require, to be constituted, the illumination or the teaching of "

inner teacher; It is rather an effort to free oneself; whence the possibility of error and evil. On the contrary, wisdom has its seat in higher reason and judges everything from the point of view of "eternal reasons" or divine ideas; It is the fruit of the illumination of the Word and thus implies perfect humility and total detachment from oneself and from everything created, excluding all greed and all pride. On the other hand, the soul that possesses it does not have to sacrifice science, because it is necessary for wisdom, which must guide us through temporal things towards eternal life; Furthermore, consideration of creatures is the normal path to achieving contemplation of eternal truths. Thus, science is transformed and becomes excellent knowledge, giving up being queen to become an assistant to wisdom. Between the two, but closer to wisdom than science, is spiritual intelligence. Like wisdom, to which it is closely linked, it is distinguished from science by its direct object, which is divine truth. Spiritual intelligence is in a straight line the perfection of faith; It is not, like this, a pure "acceptance" of revealed truth; It is also a certain "understanding", relative without a doubt, but true; simple, on the other hand, like any view of intelligence properly speaking, more penetrating, despite the limits imposed by faith, subsisting as long as man lives on earth. Instead of clarifying the faith from the outside, so to speak, it encompasses it with a direct glance and understands it more or less deeply, according to the acuity of supernatural vision that is given to each one 2 '. In short, faith gives us the total truth, but in a still veiled and blind way. Intelligence and wisdom reveal meaning to us: the first, through a simple view, above all speculative; the second, by a value judgment directly inspired by charity, which unites us directly to God. It is seen that these Augustinian notions do not make full sense except when considered from the supernatural and even mystical point of view of our life of union with God. However, since Saint Augustine never excludes the natural point of view, it is possible, without distorting them, to give them a philosophical meaning. But it would take too long to go into that demonstration, and we assume that the translator of De libero arbitrio will do so, in some commentary on the second book.

Among the disciples of Saint Augustine, several, and in particular Saint Bonaventure, have maintained, even in philosophy, the distinction between science and wisdom. In his eyes, rational speculations do not in themselves have the value of infallible truth;

They acquire it by their submission to supernatural wisdom, with which they constitute a single science. Saint Thomas better distinguishes the two orders, of grace and reason. From the supernatural point of view, the entire Augustinian doctrine is fully assimilated, and by the distinctions we have just talked about, it characterizes the three gifts of the Holy Spirit: science, intelligence and wisdom 28. From the natural point of view, it adopts the notions of Aristotelian philosophy, and, for him, human science, especially philosophical science, has its autonomy and its own value of infallible truth. On the other hand, in The Master, the distinction between the three aspects of perfect knowledge does not yet appear clearly. Science and intelligence there are, more or less, identified, because they have the same object: "Omne quod intelligo, scio," says Saint Augustine; and it is not about wisdom. Its purpose is only to oppose imperfect belief, given by words and human teachers, to the possession of the immutable truth, given by the Master within; This is science or intelligence, the fruit of true teaching, which only Christ can dispense, and, consequently, in its full expansion, it is nothing more than wisdom. As to its extension, it seems to embrace all infallible, rational and supernatural eternal truths; but, compared to faith, it has a more restricted field, because "Non omne quod credo," says Saint Augustine, "etiam intelligo" 29, and here we again find the theory according to which all truth, both philosophical and theological, is a gift of faith. In this philosophical order, we have here, expressed in a lapidary form, the Augustinian method, very different from the Thomist: "Quod ergo intelligo, id etiam credo": all truth understood, scientifically possessed by philosophy, belongs to the field of faith. For Saint Thomas, on the contrary, all scientifically known truth does not belong to the field of faith. 17. Office of the teacher according to Saint Augustine and Saint Thomas.—Saint Thomas, in question 11 of De veritate, examines the problem of the teacher; The first article deals with Saint Augustine's thesis: "Can a man teach and call himself a teacher, or only God can?" The Thomistic response is in harmony with Augustinian doctrine, all inspired by the psychology of Aristotle.

Our intelligence, being at first in ignorance, must acquire science by passing from power to act; but the cause of this passage is not primarily outside us, in sensible objects or in the human teacher; It is immanent to the soul and can even be completely overcome without the help of other men. This active power, the source of science in us, is
Cough. 2-2 q. 8. 9, and q. 45. C. l l n.57.

above all the agent understanding, the faculty of the soul (of the spirit or men.s, Saint Augustine would say), which is, therefore, an innate intellectual light; and so are the first principles, which are not, it is true, innate in the proper sense, but they are not the fruit of teaching either. It is through these first principles that we acquire the sciences, extending intellectual light to new conclusions, whether from experience or by comparing known truths with each other. Now this intellectual light is a participation in the divine light of eternal truths; It is truly what Saint Augustine calls divine illumination; and this is how Saint Thomas accepts the conclusion of The Master: the Master who, above all, communicates to us! Science is God, who lives within us. Saint Thomas also highlights the role of the human teacher. He compares him to the doctor, who, without being able to produce health, comes to the aid of nature and puts it in the best dispositions to deploy its vital forces. Thus the human teacher comes to the aid of the disciple's intelligence, showing him with his words the path to the truth, which he himself must discover. The help of the teacher is of the same order as that of sensible objects, which supply the agent understanding with the matter of its abstractions and are true instrumental causes of thought; One can even say that he is more effective, due to the fact that his words are closer to producing science than the sensible things that exist outside the soul, insofar as they are signs of intelligible intentions. From this point of view, Saint Thomas specifies some arguments of The Master. Either, says Saint Augustine, we know the thing about which we are spoken, and we learn nothing, or else we ignore it, and then we do not reach the significance of the words that could instruct us; anyway we don't learn anything (n.36). Saint Thomas responds with a triple alternative: we know the thing, more in general, and the teaching brings us to a more precise knowledge; As if we are taught what man is, it is appropriate that we know something about him, namely, the reason of animal or substance or at least of being itself, which cannot be unknown to us. And yet, "how can I believe that I am instructed by my language," says Saint Augustine, "who could, if asked, explain before me what I speak, what I want to tell him?" (n.40).

And Saint Thomas notes that the disciple would answer about the first principles, but not about the conclusions, which he has not yet learned; in such a way that he does not learn the teacher's principles, but only the conclusions. Or, if he discovers these conclusions, it is thanks to the help of the teacher, as has been said more

above. The role of human teaching is thus well established. On the other hand, Saint Augustine does not deny this usefulness of language, which, he says, "if it is well understood, is not small." But its purpose was to show the other aspect of the problem, the independence of thought and its direct submission to the sole divine light, and on this point it can be said that the two great doctors are in complete agreement. 18. Ag.—Tell me what each word means. Ad.—I know what yes means, but I can't find another word that can express its meaning. Ag.—At least, do you know where what this word means resides? Ad.—You hold me too tight; but he warns that, when we do not have to express something, it is complete nonsense to utter any word; and I believe that you, when you speak to me now, do not say any words in vain, but that all that come out of your mouth you offer me as a sign, so that I may understand something; Therefore you should not utter these two syllables, if you meant nothing with them. But if, on the contrary, you believe that their enunciation is necessary, and that with them we learn or remember something when they ring in our ears, you will certainly also see what I mean, and that I do not know how to explain. Ad.—I would walk a little faster, so that, once your question was over, you would notice it through something new; and yet I would have done no more than what I had to show you. Ag.—Do you know that it is one thing to walk and another to hurry? Because neither he who walks constantly hurries, nor does he who hurries always walk, since we also say that one hurries while reading, writing and doing many other things. Therefore, by doing more quickly what you were doing before, I would believe that walking is nothing other than hurrying; you had only added this, and, therefore, it would deceive me. Ad.—I confess that we cannot show anything without a sign, if, when we are doing it, we are asked about it; because, if we do not add anything, the person who asks will believe that we do not want to teach it to him, and that, despising him, we continue in what we were doing. If, on the contrary, he asks about something we can do—and does not ask when we are doing it—we can teach him what he is asking, doing it, of course, more with the thing itself than with a sign. But if you ask me what it means to speak when I am speaking, everything I tell you to teach you must necessarily be speaking; I will continue instructing him until I make it clear to him what he wants, without departing from what he wants me to teach him, nor using other signs to demonstrate to him than the thing itself. IF THE SIGNS ARE NECESSARY TO SHOW THE SIGNS

7. Ag.—You reason very sharply; So, see if we agree that we can show without signs what we do not do when we are asked, and which, however, we can do immediately, or what, perhaps, we do as signs. Well, when we are speaking, we make signs, which is where the word signify comes from. Ad.—We agree. Ag.—Therefore, some signs can be shown with others when a question is asked about some sign. But when questions are asked about things that are not signs, they can be shown either by asking them after the question—if they can be asked—or by manifesting some sign by which they can be known. Ad.—That's right. Ag.—So, then, we first consider, in this tripartite division, if it pleases you, that the signs are shown with the signs; Are words only signs? Ad.—No% Ag.—It seems to me that, when we speak, we indicate words with words, or other signs, as if we were saying gesture or letter—since the things that these two words mean are signs, however—or something else other than a sign, as when we say stone; This word is a sign because it means something, without it being a sign what it means.
