Nam et illud, si, quod in capite habet abs te propositus versus, et hoc, ex, de quo iam diu agents in haec duce ratione pervenimus, verba sunt, nec tamen nomina; et talia fines inveniuntur.

Quamobrem cum omnia nomina verba sint, non autem omnia verba nomina sint, planum esse arbitrar quid inter verbum distet et nomen, id est inter signum signi eius quod nulla alia signa significat, et signum signi eius quod rursus alia significat. Aug.—Concedisne omnem equum animal esse, nec tamen omne animal equum esse? Ad.—Quis dubitaverit? Aug.—Hoc ergo inter nomen et verbum, quod inter equum et animal interest. Nisi forte ab assentiendo id te revocat, quod dicimus et alio moda verbum, quo signifitur ea quae per tempora declinantur, ut scribo scripsi, lego legi, quae manifestum est non esse nomina.

Ad.—That was what made me doubt. Ag.—Don't keep this indecisive. For we universally call all things that signify something, among which we count words, signs. We also say military signs (insignias)—so appropriately called—which do not contain any words. And yet, if I told you: just as every horse is an animal, but not every animal is a horse, so every word is a sign, but not every sign is a word, I think you would not hesitate for a moment. Ad.—I already understand, and fully agree, that there is the same difference between the word in general and a name as between an animal and a horse. 10. Ag.—Do you also know that, when we say animal, this trisyllabic name, which is uttered by the voice, is one thing, and what is meant by it is another? Ad.—I have already previously granted this about all signs and signifiers. Ag.—Does it seem to you that all signs mean something different from what they are, like this three-syllable animal name in no way means what it is itself? Ad.—Certainly not; Well, when we say sign, it not only means all that there are, but it means itself; because it is a word, and, without a doubt, all words are signs. Ag.—Well, isn't it true that something similar happens in this disyllable, when we say verbum? Because if this disyllable means everything that the articulation of the voice utters with some meaning, it must also be included in this species. Ad.—Dixisti omnino quod me dubitare faciebat. Aug.—Ne te istud moveat. Dicimus enim et signa universalíter omnia quae signifiant aliquid, ubi etiam verba esse invenimus. Dicimus itera signa militaría, quae iam proprie signa nominantur, quo verba non pertinent. Et tamen si tibi dicerern, ut omnis equus animal, non autem omne animal equus est, ita omne verbum signum, non autem omne signum verbum est, nihil, ut opinor, dubitares. Ad.—Iam intelligo, et prorsus assentior, hoc interesse inter uníversale illud verbum et nomen, quod inter animal et equum. 10. Aug.—Scisne etiam, cum dicimus: Animal, aliud esse hoc trisyllabum nomen, quod voce prolatum est, aliud id quod significatur? Ad.—Iam hoc supra concessi de omnibus signis et significabilibus. Aug.—Num omnia signa tibi videntur aliud significare quam sunt, sicut hoc trisyllabum, cum dicimus: Animal, nullo moda idem significat quod est ipsum?

Ad.—Non «ane: nam cum dicimus: Signum, non solum signa caetera quaecumque sunt, sed etiam seipsum significat; est enim verbum, et utique omnia verba signa sunt. Aug.—What? in hoc disyllabo cum dicimus: Verbum, nonne tale aliquid contingit? Nam si omne quod cum aliquo significatu articulata voce profertur, hoc disyllabo significatur, etiam ipsum hoc genere includitur.

Ad.—That's right. Ag.—Well, doesn't it also have a name? Because it means the names of all genders, and itself is a name of the neutral gender. Or is it that, if I asked you what part of speech the name is, could you correctly answer me except by saying name? Ad.—It is true. Ag.—Therefore, there are signs that, among the other things that they signify, signify themselves. Ad.—Yes. Ag.—Do you think that this four-syllable sign, when we say coniunctio (conjunction), belongs to this category? Ad.—Not at all; because the things it signifies are not names, while it is a name. CHAPTER

11. Ag.—You have reasoned well; Now see if there are signs that signify each other, in such a way that, as one signifies this one, so this one signifies that one; Well, this four-syllable, when we say coniunctio, and those words that it means, when we say if, or, then, but, then, because and other similar words, do not have a mutual meaning, because that single word means all of these; but there is none among the latter that can mean that four syllable. Ad.—Ita est. Aug.—What? nomen nonne similiter habet? Nam et omnium generum nomina significat, et ipsum nomen generis neutri nomen est. An, si ex te quaererem quae pars orationis nomen, posses mihi I will respond recte, nisi nomen? Ad.—Verum dicis. Aug.—Sunt ergo signa quae Inter alia quae signifiant et seipsa significent. Ad.—Sunt. Aug.—Num tale tibi videtur hoc quadrisyllabum signum cum dicimus: Coniunctio? Ad.—Nullo moda: nam ea quae significat, non sunt nomina; hoc autem nomen est. CAPUT

11. Aug.—Bene attendisti: nunc illud vide, utrum inveniantur signa quae se invicem significant, ut quemadmodum hoc ab illo, sic illud ab hoc significetur: non enim ita sunt Inter se hoc quadrisyllabum, cum dicimus: Coniunctio, et illa quae ab hoc significantur, cum dicimus: Si, vel, nam, namque, nisi, ergo, quoniam, et similia; nam haec illo uno significatur, nullo autem horum unum illud quadrisyllabum significatur.

Ad.—I see it, and I want to know what signs these are whose significance is reciprocal. Ag.—Do you not know then that, when saying word and name, we say two names? Ad.—I know. Ag.—Huh? Do you not know that, when saying name and word, we say two names? Ad.—I also know this. Ag.—Do you know, then, that a word can mean as much to a name as a name can mean to a word? Ad.—I agree. Ag.—Can you say the difference between them, except for their diversity in writing and pronunciation? Ad.—Perhaps I can, because I see that it is the same thing that I said a little. When we say words, we mean everything that the articulation of the voice utters with some meaning; Consequently, every name, and the term name itself, is a word; but not every word is a name, even if the term nalabra is a name. 12.—Ag.—And if someone affirms and proves to you that, just as every name is a word, so every word is a name, will you be able to find out how they differ, apart from the different sounds of their letters? Ad.—I won't be able to, and I judge that it doesn't make any difference. Ag.—And if everything that the articulation of the voice utters with any meaning are words and names, but they are Ad.—Video, et quaenain signa sint se invicem significantia, cupio cognoscere. Aug.—Tu ergo nescis cum dicimus: Nomen et verbum, duo verba tell us? Ad.—Scio. Aug.—What? illud nescis, cum dicimus: Nomen et verbum, duo nomina tell us? Ad.—Id quoque scio. Aug.—Six igitur tam nomen verbo, quam etiam verbum nomine significari. Ad.—Assentior. Aug.—Potesne dicere, except eo quod diverse scribuntur et sonant, quid inter se differant? Ad.—Possum fortasse; nam id esse video quod paulo ante dixi. Verba enim cum dicimus, omne quod articulata voce cum aliquo significatu profertur, significamus; unde omne nomen, et ipsum cum dicimus: Nomen, verbum est: at non omne verbum nomen est, quamvis nomen sit, cum dicimus: Verbum. 12. Aug.—Quid, si quisquam tibi affirmet et probet, ut omne nomen verbum est, ita omne verbum nomen esse? poterisne invenire quid distent, praeter diversum in litteris sonum? Ad.—Non potero, nec omnino distare aliquid, puto. Aug.—Quid, si omnia quidem quae voce articulata cum aliquo significatu proferu'ntur, et verba sunt et nomina; thirst also for cause

for one reason words and for another names, won't there be any difference between a name and a word? Ad.—I don't understand how this could be. Ag.—At least you understand that every red thing is visible, and that every visible thing is red, although these two words mean differently and differently. Ad.—I understand. Ag.—If this is so, consequently every word is a name and every name is a word, although these two names or two words, that is, the terms name and word, have different meanings. Ad.—I see that this can happen, but I hope you will show me how it happens. Ag.—You notice, as I believe, that everything that, meaning something, emerges through the articulation of the voice, hurts the ear to awaken the sensation and is transmitted to the memory to give knowledge. Ad.—I warn you. Ag.—Therefore, two things happen when we utter something with such a voice. Ad.—That's right. Ag.—Why has one of these two things been called verbum (word) and the other nomen (name)? Is it not for the reason that the term verbum is derived from verberare (to hurt) and the term nomen is derived from noscere (to know), since the former is addressed to the ear and the latter to the spirit? 13. Ad.—I will assent to it when you show me how we can rightly call all words names? verba et alia de causa nomina sunt? nihilne distabit inter nomen et verbum? Ad.—Quomodo istud sit non intelligo. Aug.—Hoc saltem intelligis, omne coloratum visibile esse, et omne visibile coloratum, quamvis haec duo verba distincte differenterque significent. Ad.—Intelligo. Aug.—Quid si ergo ita et omne verbum nomen, et omne nomen verbum est, quamvis haec ipsa duo nomina, vel duo verba, id est nomen et verbum, difíerentem habeant significationem? Ad.—Iam video posse id accidere: sed quomodo id accidat, exspecto ut ostendas. Aug.—Omne quod cum aliquo significatu articulata voce prorumpit, animadvertis, ut opinor, et aurem verberare, ut sentimenti; et memoriae mandari, ut nosci possit. Ad.—Animadverto. Aug.—Duo ergo quaedam contingunt cum aliquid tali voce proferimus. Ad.—Ita est. Aug.—Quid, si horum duorum ex uno appellata sunt verba, ex altero nomina; verba scilícet a verberando, nomina vero a noscendo, ut illud primum ab auribus, hoc autem secundum ab animo vocari meruerit? 13. Ad.—Concedem, cum ostender!9 quomodo recte possimus omina verba nomina dicere.

Ag.—It is easy, since I believe you have learned and retained that the pronoun is called that because it is in place of the name itself, and yet it expresses a reality with a less full meaning than the name. Well, as I believe, this is how the author you have recited in grammar defined it: "Pronoun is a part of the sentence that, used in place of the name, means the same thing as the name, although with less force." Ad.—I remember it and approve it. Ag.—You see, therefore, that, according to this definition, we can only use pronouns for names and to replace them, as when we say: this man, the same king, the same woman, this gold, that silver; The terms this, the same, the same, this, that, are pronouns; man, king, woman, gold. silver, are names, which mean things more strongly than those. Ad.—I see it and I agree to it. Ag.—Now tell me some conjunctions, whatever you want. Ad.—Because, and, well, but. Ag.—Does it seem to you that all these things that you have said are names? Ad.—No way. Ag.—Do you think that, at least, I have spoken correctly using the terms: all these things that you have said? Ad.—Completely well; and now I understand in what way you have shown me that I enunciated names, since otherwise it would not have been possible to say: all these things. But I fear that it seems to me that you have spoken well, because I cannot deny that these four conjunctions are also words, Aug.—Facile est: nam credo te accepisse ac tenere pronomen dictum, quod pro ipso nomine valeat, rem tamen notet minus plena significatione quam nomen. Nam, ut opinor, definivit ille ita, quem grammatico reddidisti: Pronomen est pars orationis, quae pro ipso posita nomine, minus quidem plene, idem tamen significat. Ad.—Recordor et probo. Aug.—Vides igitur secundum hanc definitionem nullis nísi nomínibus serve, et pro his solis poni posse pionomina, velut cum dicimus: Hic vir, ipse rex, eadem mulier, hoc aurum, illud argentum: hic, ipse, eadem, hoc, illud, pronomina ( esse; vir, rex, mulier, aurum, argentum, nomina, quibus plenius quam illis pronominibus res significatae Ad.—Video et assentior. Aug.—Tu ergo nunc mihi coniunctiones quaslibet enuntia.' Ad.—Non omnino Aug.—Ego. saltem tibi recte locutus videor, cum dicerem: Haec «mnia quae dixisti?

Ad.—Recte prorsus; et iam intelligo quam mirabiliter ostenderis me nomina enuntiasse: non enim aliter de his recte dici potuisset: Haec •omnia. Sed enim vereor adhuc, ne propterea mihi recte locutus videaris,

and because all these things can be said in the same way, correctly, and | all these words. And if you ask me what part of speech this expression, word, corresponds to, I will answer that it is a name. Here is why, perhaps, you added the pronoun to this name, so that your expression was correct. 14. Ag.—You are very acutely deceived; But, so that you stop deceiving yourself, pay attention even more sharply to what I am going to say, if I can say it as I want; because it is as intricate to talk about words with words as to intertwine and rub fingers with others; in which operation it is difficult and someone who knows, if not the one who performs it, which fingers are the ones that itch and which ones that try to calm the itch. Ad.—Well, you have me here with all my heart, because this similarity has made me very attentive. Ag.—Certainly I pronounce words and they consist of syllables. Ad.—That's right. Ag.—Thus, making mainly use of the authority, which is most venerable for us, when the apostle Paul says: "There was no yes and no in Christ, but only in Him there was yes," I do not think it is to be thought that these three letters, stated when we say est (yes), existed in Christ, but rather what they mean. Ad.—It is true. Ag.—You understand, therefore, that he who said: "He did exist in Him," meant only that what existed is called yes quod has quatuor coniunctiones etiam verba esse non negated; ut ideo de his recte dici potuerit: Haec omnia, quoniam recte dicitur: Haec verba omnia. Si autem a me quaeras quae sit pars orationis Verba, nihil aliud responderbo quam Nomen. Quare huic nomini fortasse pronomen adiunctum est, ut illa recta esset locutio tua. 14.

Aug.—Acute quidem falleris, sed ut fallí desinas, acíius attende quod dicam, si tamen id dicere, ut voló, valuero: nam verbis de verbis agere tam implicatum est, quam digitos digitis inserere et confricare; ubi vix dignitiescitur, nisi ab eo ¡pso qui id agit qui digiti pruriant, et qui auxilientur prurientibus. Ad.—En toto animo adsum, nam ista haec similarityo me intentissimum fecit. Aug.—Verba certe rang, et litteris constant. Ai.—Ita est. Aug.—Ergo ut ea potíssimum auctoritate utamur, quae nobis charissima est, cum ait Paulus apostolus: Non erat in Christo Est et Non, sed Est in illo erat \ non opinor, putandum est tres istas litteras, quas enuntiamus cum dicimus, est, Fuisse in Christo, sed illud potius quod istis tribus litteris significatur. Ad.—Verum dicis. Aug.—Intelligis igitur eum qui ait: Est in illo erat, nihil aliud di1

in it; as, if he had said that virtue existed in Christ, it would not be understood that he had said anything other than what was in Him called virtue; Were it not that I believed and believed that these two syllables that we enunciate when we say virtue existed in Him, and not what they mean. Ad.—I understand it and I agree with you. Ag.—What? Don't you understand that there is no difference between someone saying: "it is called virtue" or "it is named virtue"? Ad.—It is clear. Ag.—Well, it is clear that it can be said indistinctly: yes, what was in Christ is called or yes, it is named. Ad.—I see that there is no difference here either. Ag.—Do you also see what I want to show? Ad.—Not yet. Ag.—Don't you see that a name is what something is called? Ad.—There is nothing clearer for me. Ag.—You see, therefore, that yes (est) is a name, since what was in Christ is called yes. Ad.—I cannot deny it. Ag.—But if you are wondering what part of the discourse the expression est belongs to, I don't believe you would tell me that it is a name, but rather a verb, even after having shown us the reason that it is a name. Ad.—That's exactly what you say. Ag.—Do you still doubt that other parts of the sentence are names, considered in the same way that we have taught? xisse quam Est appellatur quod in illo erat: tanquam si dixisset: Virtus in illo erat; non utique aliud dixisse acciperetur, nisi virtus appellatur quod in illo erat: ne diias istas syllabas quas enuntiamus, cum dicimus: Virtus, et non illud quod his duabus syllabis significatur, in illo Fuisse arbitraremur. Ad.—Intelligo ac sequor. Aug.—What? illud nonne intelligis etiam nihil interesse utrum quisque •dicat: Virtus appellatur, an Virtus nominatur? Ad.—Manifestum est. Aug.—Ergo ita manifestum est, nihil interesse utrum quis dicat: Est appellatur, an Est nominatur quod in illo erat. Ad.—Video et hic nihil distare. Aug.—Iamne etiam vides quid velim ostendere? Ad.—Nondum sane. Aug.—Itane tu non vides nomen esse id quo res aliqua nominatur? Ad.—Hoc plane nihil certius video.

Aug.—Vides ergo, Est nomen esse, siquidem illud quod erat in illo, Est nominatur. Ad.—Negare non possum. Aug.—At si ex te quaererem quae sit pars orationis Est; non opinor nomen, sed verbum esse diceres, cum id ratio etiam nomen esse docuerit. Ad.—Ita est prorsus ut dicis. Aug.—Num adhuc dubitas alias quoque parts orationis eodem moda, quo demonstravimus, nomina esse?

Ad.—I have no doubt, since I confess that it means something. But if you ask me what they are called, that is, they are named, each of the things that they mean, I will not be able to answer you except by stating those parts of the sentence that we do not call names, or better, as I see, that we are forced to call them 15. Ag.—Does there not be anything to oppose, so that there is no one who throws our reasoning to the ground, saying that the authority of doctrine and not of words must be attributed to the Apostle, and, therefore, that The foundation, on which our persuasion rests, is not as firm as we believe, since it may happen that Paul, despite the purity of his life and his doctrine, has spoken with less righteousness when he said: “The yes was in Christ; all the more so as he confesses himself to be uneducated in language"? How do you think this argument can be refuted? Ad.—I have nothing to oppose, and I ask you to look for one of those who are recognized as having a great knowledge of words, with whose authority you will better obtain what you want. Ag.—You judge that reason, without the testimony of authority, has no force to demonstrate that all the parts of the sentence mean something, and that that thing is called according to its meaning, and if it is called, it is also named, and if it is named, it must be named by some name, and yet this is easily understood by examining the various languages. Because who does not see that the Greeks, when asked what name they give to what we call who (quis), have to answer yes; asked what they call what we want Ad.—Non dubito, quandoquidem fateor ea significare aliquid. Si autem res ipsae quas signifiant, quid singulae appellentur, id est nominentur, interrogates; I will answer non possum, nisi eas ipsas parts orationis, quas nomina non vocamus, sed, ut cerno, vocare convincimur. 15. Aug.—Nihilne te movet, ne quis existat qui nostram istam rationem labefactet saying, Apostólo non verborum, sed rerum auctoritatem esse tribuendam; quamobrem fundamentum persuasionis huius non tam esse firmum quam putamus: fieri enim posse ut Paulus quamquam vixerit praeceperitque rectissime, minus tamen recte locutus sit, cum ait: Est in illo erat; praesertim cum se ipse imperitum sermone fateatur? 2 quo tandem moda istum refellendum arbitraris? Ad.—Nihil habeo quod contradicam, et te oro ut aliquem de illis reperias, quibus verborum notitia summa conceditur, cuius auctoritate potius id quod cupis efficias.

Aug.—Minus enim tibi videtur idenea, remotis auctoritatibus, ipsa ratio, qua demonstratur omnibus partibus orationis significari aliquid, et ex eo appellari; si autem appellari, et nominan; If they nominate, nonne utique nominari: quod in diversis linguis facillime iudicatur. Quis enim non videat, si quaeras quid graeci nominent quod nos nominamus Quis, I will respond TÍS; quid graeci nominent quod nos nominamus He flew,

(flew), they must answer QéAco; When asked what they call what we call bene, they will answer vocAcos; When asked what they call what we write (scriptum), they have to answer TO yeypccuuévov; how they call what we and (et), have to answer
KCCÍ; how do they call what we from (ab),

reply closed; asked what they call what we, oh! (heu), they have to respond I heard; And who sees that in all these parts of the sentence that I have just stated, the one who asked has spoken correctly? Which would be impossible if those parts were not names. Now, being able to understand in this way, without any authority from the eloquent, that the apostle Paul has spoken correctly, what need do we have to seek the opinion of an author to corroborate our own? 16. But in order that no slow-witted or ill-willed man should fail in his prayers, and affirm that he will not yield in any way, except with the authority of those to whom the common voice attributes the laws of words, who can there be, among the Latin writers, of more authority than Cicero? Well, in his very famous Verrinas, he called the word coram (in front of) a name, although in that place it is a preposition or adverb. However, because it may happen that I do not understand that passage perfectly, and it may be explained in a different way on another occasion, either by me or by another, I do not entertain myself in thinking to which the yes (est) may correspond. For the most famous teachers in the art of discussion teach that the perfect sentence consists of a noun and a verb, which can be affirmative or negative; This same class is called by Tullius a proposition in one passage; and when the verb is in the third person, they say that the noun must be in the nominative, agreeing with it; and they say well; because, I would answer 6éAw; quid graeci nominent quod nos nominamus Bene, I will respond KCAÜS; quid graeci nominent, quod nos nominamus Scriptum, responderi TO yeypccuuévov; quid graeci nominent quod nos nominamus Et, responderi KCCÍ; quid graeci nominent quod nos nominamus Ab, responderi cnró; quid graeci nominent quod nos nominamus Heu, responderi oí; atque in his omnibus partibus orationis, quas mine enumeravi, recte loqui eum qui sic interroget; quod, nisi nomina essent, fieri non posset? Hac ergo ratione Paulum apostolum recte locutum esse, cum remotis omnium eloquentium auctoritatibus obtinere possimus; quid opus est quaerere cuius persona sententia nostra fulciatur? 16. Sed ne quis tardior aut imprudentior nondum cedat, asseratque, nisi illis auctoribus, quibus verborum leges consensu omnium tribuuntur, nullo moda esse cessurum; quid in latina lingua excellentius Cicerone inveniri potest?

At hic in suis nobilissimis orationibus quas Verrinas vocant, Coram, praepositionem, sive illo loco adverbium sit, nomen appellavit. Verumtamen quia fieri potest ut ego illum locum minus bene intelligam, exponaturque alias aliter, vel a me vel ab alio; est ad quod responderi posse nihil puto. Tradunt enim nobilissimi disputationum magistri, nomine et verbo plenam constare sententiam, quae affirmari negarique possit: quod genus Idem Tullius quodam loco pronuntiatum vocat: et cum verbi tertia persona est, nominativum cum

If you reflect with me on that, you will know, I believe, that there are two propositions when we say: the man is sitting, the horse is running. Ad.—I know him. Ag.—Do you see that on each one of them there is a name: man and horse; and in each one, likewise, a verb: is he sitting and running? Ad.—I see it. Ag.—Then if I only said: he is sitting, or he is running, with great reason you would ask me who or what, so that I could answer you: a man, or a horse, or an animal, or anything else that could complete with a name the proposition stated by the verb, that is, that sentence that can be affirmative or negative. Ad.—I understand. Ag.—Attend to the rest, and suppose we see something there in the distance, and we don't know if it is an animal or a stone, or something else, and I tell you: because it is a man, it is an animal; Wouldn't he speak recklessly? Ad.—Very recklessly, but you would not say it so recklessly if you said: if he is a man, he is an animal. Ag.—You speak rightly; So, then, I like the yes in your sentence; You also like it; and we both dislike why he licked it. Ad.—I agree. Ag.—Examine whether these two sentences are complete propositions: please the yes, dislike the why. Ad.—Complete in all respects. ea casum nominis aiunt esse oportere; et recte aiunt: quod mecum si consideres, velut cum dicimu«: Homo sedet, Equus currit, agnosois, ut opinor, duo esse pronuntiata. Ad.—Agnosco. Aug.—Cernís in singulis singula esse nomina, in uno homo, in altero equus; et verba singula, in uno sedet, in altero currit? Ad.—Cerno. Aug.—Ergo si dicerem, sedet tantum, aut currit tantum, recte a me quaereres, quis vel quid; ut will respond: Homo, vel equus, vel animal, vel quodlibet aliud, quo possit nomen redditum verbo implere pronuntiatum, id est illam sententiam quae affirmari et deniali potest. Ad.—Intelligo. Aug.—Attende caetera, et finge nos videre aliquid longius, et incertum habere utrum animal sit an saxum, vel quid aliud, meque tibi dicere: Quia homo est, animal est; nonne I will be afraid to say?

Ad.—Temeré omnino: sed non temeré plañe díceres: Si homo est, animal est. Aug.—Recte dicis. Itaque in locutione tua placet mihi Si; placet et tibi: utrique autem nostrum in mea displicet Quia. Ad.—Assentior. Aug.—Vide iam utrum istae duae sententiae plena pronuntiata sint: Placet Si, displicet Quia. Ad.—Plena omnino.

Ag.—Come on, tell me now which are verbs and which are nouns. Ad.—I think the verbs are likes and dislikes; and names, what else can they be that yes and why? Ag.—Then it is sufficiently proven that these two conjunctions are names. Ad.—Yes, sufficiently. Ag.—Can you yourself demonstrate the same in the other parts of the sentence, according to this rule? Ad.—I can.
SIGNS THAT MEAN THEMSELVES

17. Ag.—Let us leave this now, and tell me if it seems to you that, just as we have noted that all words are names and all names are words, so all names are words and all words are names. Ad.—I do not see that between these various things there is any difference other than the different sound of the letters. Ag.—Neither do I contradict you for now, although there is no shortage of those who distinguish them in meaning, and which and what appears it is not necessary for us to consider now. But you certainly realize that we have arrived at the signs that signify each other, differing only in sound, and that signify themselves with the remaining parts of the sentence. Aug.—Age nunc, dic mihi quae ibi sint verba, quae nomina. Ad.—Verba ibi video esse, placet, et, displicet: nomina vero quid aliud quam, si, et, quia? Aug.—Has ergo duas coniunctiones etiam nomina esse satis probatura est. Ad.—Prorsus satis. Aug.—Potesne ipse per te in allus partibus orationis hoc Idem ad eamdem regulam docere? Ad.—Possum. CAPUT SIGNA

17. Aug.—Transeamus ergo hinc, et iam dic mihi utrum sicut omnia verba nomina, et omnia nomina verba esse comperimus, ita tibi et omnia nomina vocabula, et omnia vocabula nomina esse videantur. Ad.—Plane inter haec quid distet praeter diversum syllabarum sonum non video. Aug.—Nec ego interim resisto, quanquam non desint qui etiam significatione ista discernunt, quorum sententiam modoconsidere non opus est. Sed certe animadvertis ad ea iam signa nos pervenisse, quae se invicem significant, nulla praeter sonum distantia, et quae seipsa significant cum caeteris omnibus partibus orationis.

Ad.—I don't understand it. Ag.—Then you do not understand that the name is signified by the word, and the word by the name; and this in such a way that they differ in nothing except in the sound of the letters, at least for the name taken in a general way; because of the name taken in a particular way we say that it is among the eight parts of the sentence, so that it does not contain the other seven. Ad.—I understand. Ag.—Well, this is what I expressed when I said that the word ablo and the name signify each other. 18. Ad.—I know; But I ask you what you meant with these words: "That they also mean themselves with the other parts of the sentence." » Ag.—Have we not been shown by the previous reasoning that all parts of speech can be called names and words, that is, that they can be signified by a name and a word? Ad.—That's right. Ag.—If I ask you what you call the same name, that is, the sound expressed with the two syllables name, will you not answer me correctly: name? Ad.—Correctly. Ag.—Is this sign that we enunciate with four syllables meant when we say: coniunctio (conjunction)? Because this name cannot be counted among the words it means. Ad.—I admit it well.

Ag.—This is what was said when saying that the name is meant with the others that it means, which you must understand for yourself about the word. Ad.—It is now easy for me to understand; Now it occurs to me that the name is taken in a general way and in a particular way, and the word is not counted among the eight parts of the sentence; So it seems to me that this is another difference, in addition to the different sound. Ag.—Well, do you think there is any other difference between nomen (name) and óvonct than the sound, by which the Latin and Greek languages ​​are also distinguished? Ad.—I don't see any other difference. Ag.—We have, then, arrived at the signs that signify themselves and one another, and what this one means, also that one, and which are only differentiated in sound; In fact, we have now found this fourth category, because the previous three relate to the name and the word. Ad.—We have already arrived.

Ad.—Non intelligo. Aug.—Non ergo intelligis et nomen vocabulo et vocabulum nomine signify; et ita ut praeter sonum litterarum nihil intersit, quantum •ad generale nomen pertinet: nam et speciale nomen dicimus, quod inter octopartes orationis ita est, ut alias septem non contineat. Ad.—Intelligo. Aug.—At hoc est quod dixi, se invicem significare vocabulum et nomen. 18. Ad.—Teneo, sed quaero quid dixeris: Cum etiam seipsa significant cum alus partibus orationis. Aug.—Nonne superior ratio docuit nos, omnes parts orationis, et nomina posse dici et vocabula, id est et nomine et vocabulo posse significan? Ad.—Ita est. Aug.—What? ipsum nomen, id est sonum istum duabus syllabis expressum, si ex te quaeram quid appelles, nonne recte mihi responderbis: Nomen? Ad.—Rect. Aug.—Num ita se significat hoc signum quod quatuor syllabis enuntiamus cum dicimus: Coniunctio? Hoc enim nomen inter illa quae significat, numeran non potest. Ad.—Recte accipio.

Aug.—Id est quod dictum est nomen -seipsum significare cum alus quae significat; quod etiam de vocabulo licet per teipsum intelligas. Ad.—Iam facile est: sed illud mihi nunc venit inmentem, nomen et generaliter et specialiter dici; vocabulum autem inter octopartes orationis non accipi: quare hoc quoque inter se praeter diversum sonum differre arbitror. Aug.—What? nomen et óvoua distare inter se aliquid putas praeter sonum. quo etiam linguae discernuntur latina atque graeca? Ad.—Hic vero nihil aliud intelligo. Aug.—Perventum est ergo ad ea signa quae et seipsa significent, et aliud ab alio invicem significetur, et quidquid ab uno hoc et ab alio; et nihil praeter sonum inter se differant: nam hoc quartum moda invenimus; tria enim superiora, et de nomine et verbo intelliguntur. Ad.—Omnino perventum.

19. Ag.—I would like you to summarize everything we have discovered in our discussion. Ad.—I will do it according to my strength. I remember that the first thing we have looked for for some time has been why we speak, and we have found that we speak to teach
19. Aug.—Iam quae sermocinando invenerimus, velim recenseas. Ad.—Faciam quantum possum. Nam primo omnium recordor aliquandiu nos quaesisse quam ob causam loquamur, inventumque esse

to remember, since, when we ask questions, the goal we propose is that the one we question learns what we want to hear; We have added that singing, which I seem to do for pleasure, is not properly a language, and that in prayer to God, who we cannot think of as being taught or remembering something, our words have the effectiveness of reminding ourselves or awakening memory in others or instructing them. Then, having fairly determined that words are nothing other than signs, and that things that signify nothing cannot be so, you presented a verse, in order that and attempted to show the meaning of each word, which was as follows: "Si nihil ex tanta superis placeturberelinqui." »We did not find the meaning of the second word, although it is very well known and used. And, it seems to me that we do not uselessly intersperse it when speaking, but rather that with it we teach something to the listener, we agreed that perhaps it designated the affection of the mind when it finds or believes it has found that what it seeks does not exist; You certainly answered me; but, jokingly avoiding the depth of the matter, I left it to be elucidated at another time, and I no longer believe that I have forgotten your promise. Then, as I was in a hurry to explain the third word of the verse, I was led to show, rather than another word whose value was identical, the very thing that the words meant. And having heard that this could not be done by discourse, we turned to those things that are shown with the finger to those who ask.

I thought that these things were all corporeal things, but we saw that they were only the visible ones. From here» docendi commemorandive gratia nos loqui, quandoquidem nec cura interrogamus, aliud agimus quam ut ille qui interrogatur discat quid velimus audire; et in canto quod delectationis causa faceré videmur, non sit proprium locutionis; in orando Deo, quem doceri aut commemorari existimare non possumus, id verba valeant, ut vel nos ipsos commonefaciarnus, vel alii commoneantur doceanturve per nos. Deinde cum satis constitisset verba nihil aliud esse quam signa; ea vero quae non aliquid significent, signa esse non posse, proposuisti versum, cuius verba singular quid significarent, conarer ostendere: is autem erat: «Si nihil ex tanta Superis placet urbe relinqui»'. Cuius secundum verbum quamvis notissimum et manifestissimum, quid tamen significaret, non reperiebamus. Cumque mihi videretur non frustra nos id in loquendo interponere, sed quod eo aliquid twelveamus audientem; ipsam mentís affectionem, cum rem quam quaerit, non esse invenit, vel invenisse se putat, hoc verbo fortasse indicari, responderi tu quidem; sed tamen nescio quam profunditatem quaestionis ioco Evitans, in aliud tempus illustrandam distulisti: nec me debiti quoque tui oblitum putes. Inde tertium in versu verbum cum satagerem exponere, urgebar abs te, ut non verbum aliud quod idem valeret, sed rem ipsam potius quae per verba significaretur ostenderem. Cumque id sermocinantibus nobis fieri non posse dixissem, ventum est ad ea quae interrogantibus digit monstrantur.

I don't know how, we pass on to the deaf and buffoons, who signify with gesture and without words not only what can be seen, but much and almost everything that we speak; where we find that the gestures themselves are signs. Then we began to examine how we could show without any kind of signs the very things that are signified by signs, since with a sign we denote a wall, a color and all the visible things, when we show them with the finger. Here and I was wrong when I said that it was an impossible thing, and it was finally established among us that those things that we do not do at the moment when we are asked could be demonstrated without signs, and we can do them after the question; and that, however, locution was not of this kind, since, if we are speaking, we are asked what locution is, evidently it is through the same locution that shows what it is, as we have seen. 20. Because we have noticed that some signs are shown with others, or with signs other things that are not, or also without signs the things that we can do after being asked, and we take the first of these three cases to carefully consider and clarify it. In this discussion it became clear that there are signs that cannot be meant by what they mean, as, for example, the four-syllable coniunctio (conjunction); and that they can be meanings, as, for example, when saying sign we also mean a word, and when saying word we also denote a sign; because the terms sign and word are at the same time two signs and two words.

And it has been shown that, in the species of signs that Haec ergo corporalia esse omina arbi trabar, sed invmiimus sola visibilia. Hinc nescio quomodo ad surdos et histriones devenimus, qui non quae sola videri possunt, sed fina praeterea ac prope omnia quae loquimur, gestu sine voce significant; eosdem tamen gestus signa esse comperimus. Tum rursus quaerere coepimus, quomodo res ipsas quae signis signifitur, sine ullis signis valeiemus ostenditur, cum et ille paries, et color et omne visibile, quod intentione digiti ostenditur, sign quodam convinceretur ostendi. Hic ergo errans cum inveniri tale nihil posse dixissem, tandem inter nos constitit, ea posse demonstrari sine signing, quae cum a nobis quaeruntur, non agimus, et post inquisitionem agere possumus; locutionem tamen ex eo non esse genere: siquidem et loquentes cum interrogamur quid sit locutio, istam per seipsam demonstrare facile esse satis apparuit. 20. Ex quo admoniti sumus aut signis signa monstrari, aut signis alia quae signa non sunt, aut etiam sine signing res quas agere post interrogationem possumus: horumque trium primum diligentius consideradum discussiendumque suscepimus. Qua disputatione declaratum est, partim esse signa, qua ab iis signis quae significarent, significan vicissim non possent, ut est hoc quadrisyllabum cum, Coniunctio, dicimus: partim quae possent, ut cum dicimus: Signum, etiam verbum significamus; et cum dicimus: Verbum, etiam signum significamus; nam signum et verbum, et duo signa, et duo verba sunt. In hoc autem genere, quo invicem se signa significant, quaedam non tantum, quaedam

They are reciprocal, some do not have the same value, others have the same value and others, in short, are identical. Well, here is that this disyllable that sounds when we say sign means without exception everything by which anything is meant; But the term word is not a sign of all signs, but only of those emitted by the articulation of the voice. From which it is seen that, although the sign (signum) means the word (verbum) and the word the sign, that is, those two syllables to these and these to those, the sign has a greater extension than the word; That is, those two syllables mean more than these. On the contrary, the terms word and name, taken in their general meaning, have the same value. He showed the reason that all parts of speech are also names, because pronouns can be associated with them, and that all of them can be said to name something, and that there is none that, by adding a verb, cannot form a complete proposition. But although the terms name and word have the same value, since all things that are words are also names, they do not, however, have an identical value, since we have found in our discussion that for different reasons the one is called a word and the other a name. We have seen, in fact, that the word hurts the ear and that the name excites memory in the spirit; difference that we express very clearly in language, saying: What is the name of this thing that we want to record in memory? Instead of saying: the word of this thing. We have later found terms that not only have the same meaning, but are also identical, and between which there is no other difference than the sound of the letters, such as name and óvoncc. I had forgotten that in the species tantum, quaedam vero etiam idem valere monstratum est. Etenim hoc disyllabum, quod sonat cum dicimus: Signum, prorsus omnia quibus quidque significatur significat: non autem omnium signingum signum est cum dicimus: Verbum, sed tantum eorum quae articulata voce proferuntur. Unde manifestum est, quamvis et verbum sign, et signum verbo, id est et duae istae syllabae illis, et illae istis significentur, plus tamen signum valere quam verbum, plura scilicet illis duabus syllabis, quam istis signifiibus. Tantumdem autem valet generale verbum, et generale nomen.

Docuit enim ratio omnes parts orationis etiam nomina esse, quod et pronomina his addi possunt, et de ómnibus dici potest quod aliquid nominent, et mile earum sit quae non verbo adiuncto pronuntiatum possit implere. Sed cum tantumdem valeant nomen et verbum, eo quod omnia quae verba sunt, sint etiam nomina; non tamen idem valent. Alia quippe de causa verba, et alia nomina nuncupari, satis probabiliter disputatum est. Siquidem alterum horum ad auris verberationem, alterum ad animi commemorationem notandam esse compertum, vel ex hoc intelligi potest, quod in loquendo rectissime dicimus: Quod est huic rei nomen, rem memoriae mandare cupientes; Quod est autem huic rei verbum, dicere non solemus. Quae vero non solum tantumdem, sed etiam idem omnino significent, et inter quae nihil praeter litterarum distet sonum, nomen et Svopcc invenimus. Illud sane mihi elapsum erat in hoc genere, in quo invicem se significant, nullum nos

Of the reciprocal signs we have not found any that is not also signified among the others that it signifies. I haven't been able to remember more than this. Now you see—the only one who I believe has spoken truly and surely in this dialogue—if I have summarized well what I have said. CHAPTER

21. Aug.—Satis tu quidem memoriter omnia quae vellem recoluisti; «t, ut tibi fatear, multo evidentius mihi nunc videntur ista distincta, quam cum ea inquirendo ac disserendo de nescio quibus latebris ambo erueremus. Et tamen si dicanl vitam esse quamdam beatam. eamdemque sempiternam, que nos Deo duce, id est ipsa veritate, gra-

By certain steps appropriate to our weak step, I would fear to appear ridiculous by entering this path so sublime through the examination of signs, rather than of the things they represent. Therefore, you will forgive me if I linger with you in preliminary considerations, not to play, but to exercise the strength and acuity of the understanding, with which we can, in addition to enduring, love the warmth and light of that region in which life is blessed. Ag.—I think you would judge that I was also making fun of you if I also asked you if the first syllable of this name is something other than horn, and the second syllable something other than bre. Ad.—That's right, nothing less. Ag.—But these two syllables united form a man, will you deny it? Ad.—Who can deny it? Ag.—I ask, then, if you are these two syllables joined together. Ad.—In no way; But I see where you're pointing. dibus quibusdam infirmo gressui nostro accommodatis perduci cupiam, vereor ne ridiculus vidar, qui non rerum ipsarum quae signifitur, sed consideratione Signorum tantam viam ingredi coeperim. Dabis igitur veniam, si praeludo tecum non ludendi gratia, sed exercendi vires et mentis aciem, quibus regionis illius, ubi beata vita est, calorem ac luzem non moda sustinere, verum etiam amare possimus. Ad.—Perge potius ut coepisti: nam nunquam ego contemnenda putem quae tu divinoda vel agenda putaveris. 22. Aug.—A.ge, iam ergo illam partemconsidermus, cum signi1» non alia signa signifitur, sed ea quae significabilia vocamus. Et primum dic mihi utrum homo, homo sit.

Ad.—Never see ludas nescio. Aug.—Quid ita? Ad.—Quia quaerendum ex me censes, utrum homo aliud sit quam homo. Aug.—Ita credo te illudi arbitrareris, si etiam quaererem utrum prima huius nominis syllaba aliud sit quam, ho, et aliud secunda quam, mo. Ad.—Ita omnino. Aug.—At istae duae syllabae coniunctae, homo est: an negabis? Ad.—Quis neget? Aug.—Quaero ergo, num tu duae istae syllabae coniunctae sis. Ad.—No way: sed video quo tendas.

Ag.—Say it, then, so that you do not consider me a mocker. Ad.—Do you plan to conclude that I am not a man? Ag.—Hey! Don't you, who have admitted to be true everything that precedes and brought us to this conclusion, don't you think the same? Ad.—I will not tell you what I think, if not and I am from you about what you asked me when searching if man is a man, if these two syllables or what they mean. Ag.—Rather, answer how you understood my question; because if it is ambiguous you should have been cautious about this and not respond before being certain how I asked you. Ad.—Ambiguity matters little to me if I answer two things: man is certainly man; the two syllables are nothing more than two syllables, and what it means is nothing other than that which is. Ag.—Very good, certainly; But why have we taken in both senses what we have called man, and not the other things of which we have spoken? Ad.—How do you convince me that I have understood the rest? Ag.—To conceal other things, if you had understood my first question according to the sound of the letters, you would not have answered me anything, because it might seem to you that I had not asked anything; but now, having pronounced three words, one of which I repeated in the middle, saying utrum homo, homo sit (if the man is a man), having understood the first and last word, not according to the signs, but according to Aug.—I say ergo, ne me conüimeliosum putes. Ad.—Concludi existimas quod homo non sim. Aug.—Quid, tu non Idem existimas, qui omnia superiora ex quibus hoc confectum est, vera esse concedes? Ad.—Non tibi ego dicam quid existimem, nisi prius abs te audiero, cum quaereres utrum homo, homo sit, de duabus istis syllabis, an de re ipsa quam signifiant me interrogaveris? Aug.—Tu potius responds ex qua parte acceperis interrogationem ¡neaní: nam si est ambiguous, prius hoc cavere debuisti, ñeque mihi I will respond antequam certus rieres quonam moda rogaverim.

Ad.—Quid enim will prevent me from doing ambiguous things, cum ego ad utrum that I will respond; homo enim prorsus homo est; nam et istae duae syllabae nihil aliud sunt quam istae duae syllabae; et id quod significant, nihil aliud est, quam id quod est. Aug.—Scite hoc quidem: sed cur hoc solum quod dictum est homo, non etiam caetera quae locuti sumus, ad utrumque accepisti? Ad.—Unde enim convincor quod et caetera non sic acceperim? Aug.—Ut alia omittam, eam ipsam primam rogationem meam, si totam ex ea parte accepisses, qua syllabae sonant, nihil mihi responders; possem tibi enim videri nihil etiam interrogasse: nunc vero cum tria verba sonuerim, quorum unum in medio repetivi dices utrum homo, homo sit, primum et ultimum verbum, non secundum ipsa signa, sed secun-

What these mean is a clear sign that you thought you would answer the question with certainty and confidence. Ad.—It's true. Ag.—But why did you like to only accept the term man according to its sound and its meaning? Ad.—Behold, I now admit everything, but only as to its meaning; Well, I agree with you that we cannot speak in any way if we do not pay attention, after hearing the words, to what they are signs of. Therefore it now shows how I have deceived myself in this way of reasoning, the conclusion of which is that I am not a man. Ag.—No, but I will ask you the same thing again, so that you yourself can see where you have fallen. Ad.—Very good. 23. Ag.—I will not ask you what I had asked you first, since you have already said it. Therefore, look more carefully if the syllable hom is nothing other than hora and if the syllable bre is nothing other than bre. Ad.—Certainly, I don't see anything else. Ag.—See also if, by joining these two syllables, one becomes a man. Ad.—I will by no means agree to this; because we agree, with reason, that the sign leads our spirit towards the thing signified and that, by natural consequence of this vision, what is spoken is granted or denied. These two syllables, taken separately, have no more significance or more value than the sound that hurts our ears; That's why I conceded that they were what they sounded like.

Ag.—You think, then, and defend tooth and nail that you should not answer the questions, except according to the things meant by the words. Ad.—I don't see why this should be repugnant, as long as they are words. Ag.—I would like to know how you would respond to him—of whom we usually hear spoken of with mocking joy—who concluded that a lion had come out of the mouth of the person with whom he was arguing. Well, having asked him if what we spoke comes from our mouth, and the other being unable to deny it, he induced the man with great ease to pronounce the word lion; Once this was done, he began to mock him heavily, telling him how a good man could have expelled such a large animal, since he had confessed that everything we say comes from our mouths. Ad.—And it was not difficult to destroy this scoundrel, since I would not grant him that everything we speak comes from our mouths. Because everything we speak means to us; and the thing that is signified does not come from the mouth of the speaker, but rather the sign with which it is signified, except when the signs themselves are signified; We have already discussed this class shortly before. 24. Ag.—In this way you would be well prepared to respond to that adversary; However, what will you answer if I ask you if man is a name? Ad.—What shall I answer but that it is a name? Ag.—What? When I see you, do I see a name? Ad.—No. Ag.—Will you be still, then, while I say what follows?

dum ea quae his signifitur te accepisse, vel hoc solo manife^tum est, quod statim certus ac fidens rogationi responderdum putasti. Ad.—Verum dicis. Ad.—Ecce iam totum ex ea tantum parte qua significatur accipio: assentior enim tibi, serraocinari nos omnino non posse, nisi auditis verbis ad ea feratur animus, quorum ista sunt signa. Aug.—Vellem scire quomodo illi resistels, de quo iocantes solemus audire, quod ex eius ore cum quo disputabat, leonem processisse concluserit. Cum enim quaesisset, utrum ea quae loqueremur, our ore proceed, atque ille non potuisset denegare; quod facile Fuit, egit cum nomine, ut in loquendo leonem nominaret: hoc ubi factum est, ridicule insultare coepit et premere, ut quoniam quidquid loquimur, ore nostro exire confessus erat, et leonem se locutum esse nequibat abnuere, homo non malus tam immanem bestiam videretur vomuisse. Aug.—Bene tu quidem hoc modo adversus illum esses paratus: verumtamen mihi quid responderbis, utrum homo nomea sit requirenti? Ad.—What, even that nomen? Aug.—What? cum te video, num nomen video? Ai.—Non. Aug.—Visne igitur dicam quod sequitur?

Ad.—No, I beg you; Well, I also hear the sentence of not being a man, for having answered that it is a name when you asked me if man is a name. Well, we had agreed that it is from the thing signified that one can affirm or deny what is said. Ag.—But it seems to me that you did not give this answer without reason, because it is the law of reason, written in the depths of our spirit, that has awakened your attention. If you asked yourself what man is, you would surely answer that an animal; and if you ask yourself which part of the sentence is a man, you could not in any way answer correctly except by saying which name; Therefore, as it is seen that man is a name and is an animal, the first is said considering the sign, and the second, what the sign means. Therefore, to anyone who asks if man is a name, I will not answer but that it is; It is enough to understand that he wants to hear it considered as a sign. Ad.—I can also believe that if my man is very intelligent, shown how to walk in just a few steps, he will completely know what it is to walk. Ag.—I allow you to do it, and not opposed, but rather I help you; Well, you see that we both conclude the same thing: that certain things can be taught without the use of signs, and that what seemed true to us shortly before is false: that there is nothing at all that can be shown without signs. Now, after these, not one thing comes to mind, but a thousand things that, without any sign, can show themselves. How to doubt? I ask you. Because, without speaking of the innumerable spectacles that men represent in all theaters without signs, but with the same reality, do not God and nature expose our gaze and show for themselves this sun and the light that it sheds and dresses all things with its clarity, the moon and the other stars, the lands and the seas and everything that is born in great numbers in them? spectatorem suum docere nullo significatu, sed re ipsa, quod ille scire cupiebat? Ad.—Metuo ne quid hic tale sit, quale de illo dixi, qui quaerit quid sit ambulare. Ñeque enim video, et hic totum illud aucupium esse monstratum.

Aug.—Facile es hac cura te exuere; addo enim, si ille ita intelligens esset, ut ex hoc quod vidit, totum illud genus artis agnosceret: satis est namque ad rem, et de quibusdam rebus tametsi non ómnibus, et quosdam homines divinori posse sine Sign. Ad.—Hoc etiam ego possum illi addere; si enim sit bene intelligens, paucis passibus ambulatione monstrata, totum quid sit ambulare cognoscet. Aug.—Facías per me licet, nec tantum nihil resisto, verum etiam feveo: vides enim ab utroque nostrum id effici, ut quaedam quidam doceri sine signis queant, falsumque illud sit quod nobis paulo ante videbatur, nihil esse omnino quod sine signis possit ostendi. Iam enim ex his non unum aliquid aut alterum, sed millia rerum animo occurrunt, quae nullo sign dato per seipsa monstrentur. Quid enim dubitemus, oro te? Nam ut hominum omittam innumerabilia spectacula in omnibus theatris fine sign ipsis rebus exponentium; solem certe istum luzemque haec omnia perfundentem atque vestientem, lunam et caetera sidera, terras et maria, quaeque in his innumerabiliter gignuntur, nonne per ¡seipsa exhibitat atque otendit Deus et natura cernentibus?

33. What if you consider more carefully, perhaps you will not find anything that can be learned by its signs. When someone shows me a sign, if I don't know what it means, he can't teach me anything; But if I know it, what do I learn from the sign? The word does not show me what it means, when I read: "And their caps were not decayed" [4]. Because if this name represents certain ornaments of the head, have I, by listening to it, learned what a head is or what an ornament is? I had known them before, and I did not have knowledge of them by being named by others, but by being seen by me. Well, the first time these two syllables, caput (head), hurt my ears, I was as ignorant of what they meant as I was when I heard the name cofias read for the first time. But as they said head many times, noticing and noticing when it was said, I discovered that this was the name of a thing that sight had made me know perfectly. Before this discovery, such a word was only a sound to me; I knew it was a sign when I discovered what it was a sign of; This thing, as I said, he had not learned by meaning it to me, but by seeing it. Thus, the sign is better learned once the thing is known than the thing is learned by seeing the sign. 34. So that you may understand this more clearly, suppose that we now hear for the first time the word head, and that, not knowing whether this voice is only a sound or whether it also means something, we ask what a head is (remember that we do not want to know the thing that is meant, but rather its sign, which knowledge we certainly do not have while 33. Quod si diligentiusconsiderus, fortasse nihil invenies, quod per sua signa discatur.

Cum enim mihi signum datur, si nescientem me invenit cuius rei signum sit, docere me nihil potest: si vero scientem, quid disco per signum? Non enim mihi rem quam significat • ostendit verbum cum lego: Et saraballae eorum non sunt immutatael. Nam si quaedam capitum tegmina nuncupantur hoc nomine, num ego hoc audito, aut quid sit caput, aut quid sint tegmina didici? ante ist noveram; ñeque cum appellarentur ab alus, sed cum a me viderentur, eorum est mihi facta notitia. Etenim cum primum istae duae syllabae, cum dicimus: Caput, aures meas impulerunt, tam nescivi quid significarent, quam cum primo audirem legeremve, saraballas. Sed cum saepe diceretur: Caput notans atque animadvertens quando diceretur, reperi vocabulum esse rei quae mihi iam erat videndo notissima. Quod priusquam reperissem, tantum mihi sonus erat hoc verbum: signum vero esse didici, quando cuius rei signum esset inveni; quam quidem, ut dixi, non significatu, sed aspectu didiceram. Itaque magis signum re cognita, quam sign dato ipsa res discitur. 34. Quod ut apertius intelligas, finge nos primum nunc audire quod dicitur, caput; et nescientes utrum vox ista sit tantummodo sonans, an aliquid etiam significans, quaerere quid sit caput (memento nos non rei quae significatur, sed ipsius signi velle habere notitiam, qua caremus profecto, quamdiu cuius signum est ignoramus): si ergo ita quaeren1

We don't know what it is a sign of). Now, if our question is answered by pointing at the thing with the finger, once seen we learn the sign that we had only heard, but that we had not known. In which sign as there are two things, the sound and the meaning, we do not perceive the sound through the sign, but through the ear wounded by it, and we perceive the meaning after seeing the thing signified. Because the pointing of the finger cannot mean anything other than what the finger points to, and it points to the sign, but to the member called the head. Therefore, I cannot know by pointing the thing that I knew or the sign, at which the finger does not point. But I do not care much about the pointing of the finger, because it seems to me rather a sign of the demonstration than of the things that are demonstrated, as happens with the adverb that we call behold; Well, with this adverb we usually extend our finger, lest a new sign be enough. And mainly I am trying to persuade you, which I do not know if I will succeed, that we do not learn anything through the signs that are called words; because, as I have already said, it is not the sign that makes us know the thing, but rather the knowledge of the thing teaches us the value of the word, that is, the meaning that the sound entails. 35.

And what I have said about the head, I will also say about the ornaments and countless other things, and knowing these, however, until now I do not know such caps; If some one manifests them with the opinta gesture, or by showing me any other objects similar to them, I will not say that they have taught me - which I would easily obtain if I wanted to and or speak a little more -, but I say that the knowledge of objects colotibus res ipsa digito demonstretur, hac conspecta discimus signum quod audieramus tantum, nondum noveramus. In quo tamen sign, cum duo sint, sonus et significatio, sonum certe non per signum percipimus, sed eo ipso aure pulsata; significationem autem re, quae significatur, aspecta. Nam illa intentio digiti will mean nihil aliud potest, quam illud in quod intenditur digitus: intentus est autem non in signum, sed in membrum quod caput vocalur. Itaque per illam ñeque rem possum nosse quam noveram, ñeque signum in quod intentus digitus non est. Thirst for intentione digiti non nimis curo; quia ipsius demonstrationis signum mihi videtur potius, quam rerum aliquarum quae demonstrantur, sicut adverbium quod Ecce dicimus; nam et cum hoc adverb digitum solemus intendere, ne unum demonstrandi signum non sit satis. Et id maxime tibi nitor persuadere, si potero, per ea signa quae verba appellantur, nos nihil discere; potius enim, ut dixi, vim verbi, id est significationem quae latet in rang, re ipsa quae significatur cognita, discimus, quam illam tali significatione percipimus. 35. Et quod dixi de capite, hoc etiam de tegminibus, deque aliis rebus innumerabüibus dixerim; quas tamen cum iam noverim, saraballas illas adhuc usque non novi; quas mihi si gestu quispiam significarit aut pinxerit, aut aliquid cui similes sunt, ostenderit, non dicam non me docueiit, quod facile obtinerem, si paulo amplius loqui vellem; sed dico id quod proximum est, non verbis docuerit. Quod si eis forte conspectis

fallen in front of me does not come from words. And if, while standing and looking at them, he warns me, saying: "Here are the caps," I will learn the thing that I did not know, not by the words that are said, but by the vision of the object that has made me know and retain the value of that name. Well, I have not attested to the words of others, but to my own eyes, when learning that thing; However, I believed in those words to pay attention, that is, to investigate with my eyes what I had to see.
BUT WITH THE INTERNAL TEACHING OF THE TRUTH

36. Up to this point words have had value. Which - and I give them a lot - only encourage us to look for the objects, but they do not show them to make us know them. The one who teaches me something is the one who presents to my eyes, or to any other sense of the body, or also to intelligence, what I want to know. Therefore, with words we only learn words, or rather, the sound and noise of them. Because if everything that is not a sign cannot be a word, even if I have heard a word, I do not know what it is until I know what it means. Therefore, it is through the knowledge of things that the knowledge of words is perfected, and by hearing words, no words are learned. Because we do not learn the words we know, and we cannot confess to having learned those we do not know, unless we perceive their meaning, which comes to us not because of the fact of cum simul adero me admonuerit, they say: Ecce saraballas; discam rem quam nesciebam, non per verba quae dicta sunt, sed per eius aspectum, per quem factum est ut etiam nomen illud quid valeret, nossem ac tenerem. Non enim cum rem ipsam didici, verbis alienis credidi, sed oculis meis: illis tamen fortasse ut attenderem credidi, id est ut aspectu quaererem quid viderem. CAPUT
DISCIMUS NON VERBIS FORIS SONANTIBUS, VERITATE

36. Hactenus verba valuerunt, quibus ut plurimum tribuam, admonent tantum ut quaeramus res, non exponent ut noverimus. Is me autem aliquid docet, who vel oculis, vel ulli corporis sensui, vel ipsi etiam menti praebet ea quae cognoscere flew. Verbis igitur nisi verba non discimus, imo sonitum strepitumque verborum: nam si ea quae signa non sunt, verba esse non possunt, quamvis iam auditum verbum, nescio tamen verbum esse, doñee quid significet sciam. Rebus ergo cognitis verborum quoque cognitio perficitur; verbis vero auditis, nec verba discontur. Non enim ea verba quae novimus, discimus; aut quae non novimus, didicisse nos possumus confiteri, nisi eorum significatione percepta, quae

hearing the voices spoken, but by the knowledge of the things they mean. Reason is very true, and it is very truthfully said, that we, when words are articulated, know what they mean or we do not know: if the first thing, rather than learning, is to remember; If the second, we don't even remember, but rather we are guests looking for that meaning. 37. And if you were to say that those head ornaments, whose name we know only by sound, we cannot know them except after they have been seen - nor their name fully except after knowing them -; If you add: what we know about the three children: how they defeated the king and the llamas with their faith and their piety, what praise they sang to Pius, what honorable deference they deserved even from their enemy, have we learned it in any other way than through words? I will answer: everything that was meant in those words, we knew before. Well, I already knew what three children are, what an oven, what fire, what a king, what, finally, being preserved from fire, and everything else that those words mean. Ananias, Azariah and Mishael are as unknown to me as those caps; and these names were of no use to me nor could they be of any use to me to know them. But I confess that, more than knowing, I believe that everything that is read in that story happened at that time in the same way as it is written; and the authors, whom we attest, did not ignore this difference. For a prophet says: "If you do not believe, you will not understand"; I certainly would not have said this if I had judged that it made no difference. non auditione vocum emissarum, sed rerum significatarum cognitione contingit.

Verissima quippe ratio est et verissime dicitur, cum verba proferuntur. aut scire nos quid significant, aut nescire: si scimus, commemorari potius quam discere; si autem nescimus nec commemorari quidem, sed fortasse ad quaerendum admoneri. 37. Quod si dixeris, tegmina quidem illa capitum, quorum nomen rang tantum tenemus, non nos posse nisi visa cognoscere, ñeque nomen ipsum plenius nisi ipsis cognitis nosse: quod tamen de ipsis pueris accepimus, ut regem ac flammas fide ac religione superaverint, quas laudes Deo cecinerint, quos honores ab ipso etiam inimico meruerint, num aliter nisi per verba didicimus? Respondebo, cuneta quae illis verbis significata sunt, in our notitia iam Fuisse. Nam quid sint tres pueri, quid fornax, quid ignis, quid rex, quid denique illaesi ab igne, caeteraque omnia iam tenebam quae verba illa significant. Ananias vero et Azarias et Misael tam mihi ignoti sunt quam illae saraballae; nec ad eos cognoscendos haec me nomina quidquam adiuverunt aut adiuvare iam potuerunt. Haec autem omnia quae in illa leguntur historia, ita illo tempore facta esse, ut scripta sunt, credere me potius quam scire fateor: ñeque istam differentiam iidem ipsi quibus credimus nescierunt. Ait enim propheta - Nisi credideritis. non intelligetis1; quod non dixisset prefecto, si nihil distare iudicasset. Quod ergo intelligo, id etiam credo: at non omne quod credo, etiam intelligo. Omne autem quod intelligo, scio:

So, then, I believe everything that I understand, but I do not understand everything that I believe. And that's why I don't know how useful it is to believe many things that I don't know, for example, the story of the three children; Therefore, although I cannot know many things, I know how much usefulness can be derived from their belief. 38. Now, we understand the multitude of things that penetrate our intelligence, not by consulting the external voice that speaks to us, but by internally consulting the truth that reigns in the spirit; The words may move us to consult. And this truth that is consulted and taught is Christ, who, according to Scripture, dwells in man, that is, the unchangeable Virtue of God and his eternal Wisdom. Every rational soul consults this Wisdom; But it is revealed to each soul as much as it is capable of receiving, in proportion to its good or bad will. And if it is ever deceived, it is not because of the truth consulted, just as it is not a defect of this light that is outside that the eyes of the body have frequent illusions; We consult this light so that, as soon as we can see it, it may show us visible things.

39. If we consult the light to judge the colors, the rest that we feel through the body, the elements of this world, the bodies, our sentinon omne quod credo, scio. Nec ideo nescio quam sit utile credere etiam Fine quae nescio; cui utilitati hanc quoque adiungo de tribus pueris historiam: quare pleraque rerum cum scire non possim, quanta tamen utilitate credantur, scio. 38. De universis autem quae intelligimus non loquentem qui personat foris, sed intus ipsi mentí praesidentem consulimus veritatem, verbi« fortasse ut consulamus admoniti. lile autem qui consulitur, docet, qui in interiore homine habitare dictus est Christus, id est incommutabilis Dei Virtus atque sempiterna Sapientia 2, quam quidem omnis rationalis anima consultit; sed tantum cuique panditur, quantum capere propter propriam, sive malam sive bonam voluntatem potest. Et si quando fallitur,; ion fit vitio consultae veritatis, ut ñeque huius, quae foris est, lucis vitium est, quod corporei oculi saepe falluntur: quam luzm de rebus •visibilibus consuli fatemur, ut ea« nobis quantum cerneré valemus, ostendat.
CHRISTUS VERITAS INTUS DOCET
39. Quod si et de coloríbus luzem, et de caeteris quae per corpus sentimus, elementa huius mundi eademque corpora quae sentimus. sensusque ipsos quibus tanquam interpretibus ad talia noscenda mens

two—of which our mind uses, as interpreters, to know the matter—and if to judge intellectual things we consult, through reason, the inner truth, how can it be said that we learn in words something more than the sound that hurts the ears? For everything that we perceive, we perceive either with the senses of the body or with the mind: we give the name sensitive to the first; to the second, intelligible, or, to speak according to the custom of our authors, we call that carnal, this spiritual. We respond about the first, when questioned, if what we feel is present there; as if we are asked, when looking at the new moon, what it is and where it is. He who asks, if he does not see it, believes the words, and often does not believe; but in no way does he learn if he does not see what is said; in which he learns not by the words that were sounded, but by the things and the senses. Well, the same words that sounded to the one who did not see, sound to the one who sees. But when we are asked, not about what we currently feel, but about what we have once felt, we express not the things themselves, but the images impressed by them and recorded in our memory; In truth I do not know how we call this true, since we see it to be false; except because we narrate that we have seen and felt it, not since we see and feel it. Thus we carry those images inside our memory as documents of the things previously felt, contemplating which with right intention in our mind, we do not lie when we speak; rather, they are documents for us; Because he who listens, if he felt and witnessed them, my words do not teach him anything, but he recognizes the truth by the images that he carries with him; of his autem quae ¡intelliguntur, inteiiorem veritatem rationd consulimuí: quid dici potest unde clareat, verbis nos aliquid discere praeter ipsum qui aures percutit sonum? Namque omnia quae pereipimus, í? ut sensu corporis, aut mente percipimus. Illa sensibilia, haec intelligibilia; sive, ut more auctorum nostrorum loquar, illa carnalia, haec spiritualia nominamus. De illis dum interrogamur, responderus, si praesto sunt ea quae sentimus; velut cum a nobis quaeritur intuentibus lunam novam, qualis aut ubi sit. Hic ille qui interrogat, si non videt, ciedit verbis, et ^aepe non credit: discit autem nullo moda, nisi et ip»e quod dicitur videat; xxbi iam non verbis quae sonuerunt, sed rebus ipsis et sensibus discit.

Nam verba eadem sonant videnti quae non videnti sonuerunt. Cum vero non de lis quae coram sentimus, sed de his quae aüquando sentimus quaeiitur; non iam res ipsas, sed imagine: ab iis impressas memoriaeque mandatas loquimur: quae omnino quomodo vera dicamiis, cum false intueamur, I ignore; nisi quia non nos ea videie et sentimenté, sed vidisse ac sensisse narramus. Ita illas imagines in memoriae penetralibus rerum ante sensarum quaedam documenta gestamus, quae animo contemplantes bona conscientia non mentimur cum loquimur: sed nobis sunt ista documenta; is enim qui audit, si ea sensit atque adfuit, non discit meis verbis, sed recognoscit ablatis secum et ipse imaginibus:

same; But if he has not felt them, who will not see that he, more than learning, gives faith to the words? 40. When it comes to what we perceive with the mind, “that is, with the understanding and reason, we speak what we see is present in the interior light of truth, with which the so-called interior man is illuminated and which he enjoys; But then he who hears us also knows what I say because he contemplates it, not because of my words, if he sees it internally and with simple eyes. Therefore, I do not teach this one, who sees true things, anything by telling him the truth, since he learns, and not by my words, but by the same things that God shows him internally; therefore, if he were asked about these things, he could answer. And is there anything more absurd than to think that I teach him with my speech, when he could, when asked, explain the same things before I spoke? Well, what happens many times, that when questioned he denies something and is forced with other questions to confess it, is due to the weakness of his perception, incapable of consulting that light about the whole matter; He is warned to do it in parts when he is asked what these parts consist of that whole, which, considered in this way, he could not see. Where if he is taken by the words of the one who asks, he is taken not by words that teach, but by words that inquire in relation to his aptitude to understand the inner light; as if I were asking you if there is nothing that can be taught with words—which is what we are talking about—and to you, not being able to see everything, it would seem absurd at first sight; So, it was appropriate to ask, according to the aptitude of your strength, si autem illa non sensit, quis non eum crodrre potius verbis quam discere intelligat? 40. Cum vero de iis agitur quae mente conspicimus, id est intellectu atque ratione, ea quidem loquimur quae praesentia contuemur in illa interiore luz veritatis qua ipse qui dicitur homo interior, illustratur et fruitur: sed tune quoque noster auditor, si et ipse illa secreto ac simplici oculo videt, novit quod dico sua contemplatione, non verbis meis. Ergo ne hunc quidem twelveo vera dices, vera intuentem; Docetur enim non verbis meis, sed ipsis rebus, Deo intus pándente, manifestis: itaque de his etiam interrogatus I will answer posset. Quid autem absurdius quam eum putare locutione meadoceri, qui posset, antequam loquerer, ea ipsa interrogatus exposere?

Nam quod saepe contingit, ut interrogatus aliquid neget, atque ad id fatendum alus interrogationibus urgeatur, fit hoc imbecillitate cernentis, qui de re tota illam Lucem consulere non potest: quod ut partibus faciat, admonetur, cum de iisdem istis partibus interrogatur, quibus illa summa constat, quam totam cerneré non valebat. Quo si verbis perducitur eius qui interrogat, non tamen docentibus verbis, sed eo moda jnquirentibus, quo moda est ille a quo quaeritur, intus discere idoneus; velut si abs te quaererem hoc ipsum quod agitur, utrumnam verbis doceri nihil possit, et absurdum tibi primo videretur non valenti totum conspicere: sic ergo quaerere oportuit, ut tuae sese vires habent ad audiendum illum intus magistrum, ut dicerem: Ea quae me loquente vera esse confiteris, et certus es, et te illa nosse confirmas, unde

to hear that Master internally, to say: where have you learned what you confess to be true when I speak, and are you certain of it, and confirm that you know it? You will perhaps answer that I had taught you. Then I will add: perhaps, if I told you that I had seen a man fly, would you be as certain of my words as if you had heard that wise men are better than fools? You will certainly say no, and you will respond that you do not believe that or, even if you believe it, you ignore it; but you know this most certainly. From here you will understand, without a doubt, that you have not learned anything from my words, neither in what you did not know when I told you nor in this that you knew very well; since you would affirm, if I asked you one of those things, that you did not know the first, and that the second was known to you. But then you would fully recognize the truth that you had denied, once you knew the parts of which it is composed to be clear and certain. As for all the things we say, either the hearer is unaware that they are true, or he is not unaware that they are false, or he knows that they are true. In the first hypothesis, believe, think or doubt; in the second, he contradicts and denies; in the third, confirm; therefore, he never learns. Because those who do not know the thing after I have spoken, those who know that they have heard false things, and those who, when asked, could say the same thing that has been said, are convinced that they have not learned anything from my words. didicisti? responderes fortasse quod ego docuissem. Tum ego subnecterem: Quid si me hominem Volem vidisse dicerem, itane te certum verba mea redderent, quemadmodum si audires sapientes homines stultis esse meliores? Negares profecto et responderes, illud te non credere, aut etiamsi crederes ignorare, hoc autem certissime scire. Ex hoc iam nimirum intelligeres, ñeque in illo quod me affirmante ignores, ñeque in hoc quod optimal scires, aliquid te didicisse verbis meis; quandoquidem etiam interrogatus de singulis, et illud ignotum, et hoc tibi notum esse iurares. Tum vero totum illud quod negaveras fatereris, cum haec ex quibus constat, clear et certa esse cognosceres: omnia scilicet quae loquimur, aut ignorere auditorem utrum vera sint, aut false esse nonignore, aut scire vera esse. Horum trium in primo est credere, aut opinari, aut dubitare; in second, adversari atque renuere; in tertio attestari: nusquam igitur discere.
Quia et ille qui post verba nostra rem nescit, et qui fe falsa novit audisse, et qui posset interrogatus eadem respondere quae dicta sunt, nihil verbis meis didicisse convincitur.
THE WORD CANNOT MANIFEST WHAT WE HAVE IN THE SPIRIT

41. Therefore, in things perceived with the mind, he who cannot see them hears in vain the words of the one who sees them; except because it is useful to believe, while ignoring, such things. But everyone who can see is internally a disciple of the truth, externally a judge of the speaker, or rather of his language. Because many times you know what has been said, even if the person who said it is ignorant of it; as if someone, a supporter of the Epicureans, and who thinks that the soul is mortal, reproduces the arguments presented by the wise men in favor of its immortality, in the presence of a man capable of penetrating the spiritual; The listener will judge that the Epicurean is saying the truth, but the Epicurean does not know if what he says is true, but rather he will believe it to be very false. Are we to think, therefore, that he teaches what he does not know? And he uses the same words he could use knowing it. 42. Thus, words no longer even have the value of expressing the speaker's thoughts, since it is uncertain whether he knows what he is saying. Add those who lie and deceive, who—it is easy for you to understand—not only do they not open their soul with words, but they even cover it up. For I in no way doubt that truthful men make an effort and in some way make a profession of discovering their feelings through words, which they would achieve with everyone's applause if liars were not allowed to speak. We have frequently experienced, both in ourselves and in others, CAPUT
VERBORUM VI NE QUIDEM ANIMUS LOQUENTIS APERITUR

41. Quamobrem in iis etiam quae mente cemuntur, frustra cernentis loquelas audit quisquís ea cerneré non potest, nisi quia talia quamdiu ignorantur utile est credere: quisquís autem cerneré potest. intus est discipulus veritatis, foris iudex loquentis, vel potius ipsius locutionis. Nam plerumque scit illa quae dicta sunt, eo ipso nesciente quae dixit; veluti si quisquam epicureís credens et mortalem animam putans, eas rationes quae de immortalitate eius a prudentioribus tractatae sunt, eloquatur, illo audiente qui spiritualia contueri potest; iudicat iste eum vera dicere: at ille qui dicit, utrum vera dicat ignorat, imo etiam falsissima existimat; num igitur putandus est ea docere quae nescit? Atqui iisdem verbis utitur, quibus uti etiam sciens posset. 42.
