[1] The Aeneid.—Epic and heroic poem, written in Latin by Publius Virgilius Marón in the 1st century before Ciisto and composed of 12 books. Its subject is the enterprise, entrusted by the fates to the powerful prince Aeneas, to bring the gods of his homeland to Italy to found, with other brave Trojan heroes, a new Ilion on Latin soil. In the second book, Aeneas recounts the flight simulated by the Gypsies, the abandonment of the wooden horse they had built, the astonishment of the Trovans, who, in their obstinacy, introduced this fatal machine within their walls. He then shows how the Greeks hidden inside the horse open the door to Troy for their companions. Finally, it narrates the combat that took place in the middle of the darkness of the night, the murder of Priam, and how he himself leaves the city, sad. In his will, Virgil ordered that the manuscript of The Aeneid be burned for not having finished or corrected it; Peio Augusto resolutely opposed this determination being fulfilled, and did not allow, upon publishing the poem Tueca y Vario, a single verse to be added or removed. INTRODUCTION TO “OF THE SOUL AND ITS ORIGIN”

The origin of the soul was a problem that worried and tormented Saint Augustine throughout his life. He knew perfectly well, thanks to the lights of faith and Neoplatonic philosophy, that the soul was superior to the body. He also knew its attributes: simplicity, spirituality, immortality and its capacity to be elevated to the supernatural order of grace. But whenever in some way, direct or indirect, he made reference to its origin, his mind fluctuated between opposite solutions, remaining in his doubts and hesitations. J. Martín and E. Gilson rightly observe that it seems as if Saint Augustine had felt that this problem was in the presence of a profound mystery. For the most adequate formulation of the question, it is necessary to distinguish between the origin of Adam's soul and that of the souls of his descendants. Adam's was lovingly created by God. Saint Augustine defends it with vigor and energy and rejects any other way of appearance of the first soul 2. His concerns were about the origin of the souls of the children of Adam. We must start from the principle that it expressly denies and refutes the fact and the possibility that souls come from the emanation of the divine substance, against the Gnostics and the Manichaeans 3, or from bodily germs, against the materialist traducianism of Tertullian 4. It also excludes and combats metempsychosis and does not admit, contrary to the theories of Plato and Origen, the preexistence of souls, capable of sinning and of becoming criminals for some fault of being imprisoned in mortal bodies. How, then, does the soul appear in the new rational being? Saint Augustine addressed this question repeatedly in his works, without reaching a definitive solution \

The man who was born from the woman is not the one from whom the pot was made, but the one who was born after the union of the man and the woman, as happens today in the order of births. Therefore, if with these words the Apostle was referring to bodies, we must conclude, without any doubt, that the bodies of both sexes are the work of God. But, if our adversary limits the actual creative action of God to the soul and the spirit, it would follow that the woman was made from the man also with regard to the soul and the spirit, leaving no room to dispute those who combat the transmission of souls through generation. If, finally, he distinguishes between the body and the soul and maintains that woman came from man as regards the body and from God as regards the soul, how will the words of the Apostle be true: and everything comes from God, if the body of the woman is in such a way the work of man that it is in no way the work of man?

Therefore, preferring what the Apostle teaches to what our adversary affirms, I say that woman was made from man, either only according to the body or according to everything of which human nature consists: soul and body, not inclining for now to any of these propositions, since I still have to investigate which of them is the true one. I conclude from all this that the defenders of the transmission of souls through generation can very well admit that the part is taken for the whole in these words: Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh, the soul being understood to be understood as it is in the Word when it is said that it became flesh. Don't let me tell it or teach it to me, and I don't want you to forget it. After all, it would mean little not to believe or affirm that the soul is a part of God. Nor do we say that the Son or the Holy Spirit are a part of God, and yet we confess that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one and the same nature. It is little, for Imitate, that we do not say that the soul is a part of God: it is necessary to add that the soul is an identical nature with God. Our adversary expressed himself correctly when he said that "souls are of God's lineage by grace, not by nature," which can only be preached of faithful souls and not of all souls in general. But immediately he returned to the error he had avoided, claiming that God and the soul are of the same nature. He has not done so with those words or terms that are explicit, but it is his clear and manifest opinion; For in saying "the soul comes from God in a way that does not derive it from another nature nor the cyca of the inula, but from itself, are you not trying to teach that the soul is of the same nature as God, even though you seem to deny it with your terminology? In fact, every nature is either God, which exists by itself, or it comes from God, being its author. But, even though God is its author, some nature has not been made and another has not been made. As for the one that has not been made and, however, comes from God, or has been generated by him or proceeds from him: the one who has been generated is the only Son of God; the one who proceeds from him is the Holy Spirit, and this Trinity is of an identical substance. These three persons, in fact, are one nature.

Each one of them is God and the three together are one God, immutable, eternal, without principals: imo etiam voló ut quod didiceras, ipse dediscas. 6. I talk about these things with a Catholic, reminding him of what he already knew rather than teaching him new truths. I do not think that this is for you some new truth, some truth already heard and not believed. On the contrary, I am convinced that, by reading my letter, you recognized and recognize in its content your own faith, the faith that is common to us in the Catholic Church by God's free grant. Since, as I have indicated, I discuss these questions with a Catholic, I would like you to measure where you think the soul was taken from, not the soul of each of us, but the soul of the first man. If you believe that it was taken from nothing, that it was made and inspired or infused by the breath of God, then you believe the same as I do. But if you think it was taken-

It comes from some creature or from some pre-existing matter by the power of God, as Adam was made from the dust and Eve the rib of the first man, or as fish and birds come from the waters and terrestrial animals from the earth, in that case you are not Catholic nor are you in the truth. If, finally, you believe - which God does not allow - that the soul has been taken from nothing or from another creature, but that God made it or makes it from himself, that is, from his own nature, and this is what you learned from your young teacher, then I cannot praise art or congratulate you, since you have distanced yourself from the Catholic faith with him. Of these two errors, it would be tolerable, even though it is an error, to believe and era that God takes the souls out of another creature already made by him and pre-existing, rather than teaching that the form of his nature, because it would be horrendous blasphemy to say of the nature of God that he is mutable, that he sins, that he becomes impious and that, remaining impious to the end, he will be condemned forever. Get away from you, I beg you, brother; remove from you such an execrable error of impiety, so that you do not see yourself excluded from the number of the faithful—what God does not allow—for having allowed yourself to be seduced by a young and lay person, you, an elder and a priest, and having considered his theological nonsense as an authentic exposition of the Catholic faith. I cannot behave with you the same as with him, because your mistake, terrible, even if you have received it from him, does not deserve the compassion that his deserves. He recently entered the Catholic fold in order to find the remedy for his ravings, and you have the authority and honor that belongs to the pastors of the Church.

beginning or end. The nature that has been made is called a creature; Its creator is God, that is, the Trinity. When we say that the creature comes from God, we understand that it has not been made from his own nature. It is said to come from God because existence was received from God; but not in the sense that it was born or proceeded from him, but because it was created, formed and made by him, that is, he did not take it from any other, but directly from nothing, as he made the heaven and the earth, or rather the mass of universal matter created with the world; either that he took it from another nature already created and existing, as he formed man from the slime of the earth, woman from man and form from parents to children. However, every creature comes from God, in whatever way it is made, either by taking it out of nothing or from another creature; but he never engenders it or takes it out of himself.

And if it is false that you did this, tell me also clearly and deny such injurious rumors with your letter. I do not reproach you for having expressed your gratitude to him with such humility, provided that some usefulness could be derived from his discussion; I just want to know what you learned. Is it the case that the soul is a spirit, but a body? It does not seem to me that it is to the great detriment of Christian doctrine to ignore such absurdity, apart from the fact that subtle disputes about the various kinds of bodies are full of difficulties and are very unprofitable. If the time comes when, with the help of the Lord, this young man will write to you, as I strongly desire, perhaps you will be convinced that he did not teach you this, even though you congratulate yourself for having learned it from him. And if I instruct you on any other matter that is truly useful and necessary to faith, I pray that you may not be troubled by telling it to me. 7. 1. Anima ponió Dei non est.—St. Augustine frequently alludes to this emanatist concept, describing it as a sacrilegious error and as a great heretic and a great blasphemer to whoever holds it (cf. De anima et eius origine 1.1 c.4 n.4; c.19 n.32; 1.2 c.2 n.2; c.3 n.5-6; c.15 n.24). He had already written previously in the letter to Saint Jerome: «Non est itaquc natura incommutabilis, quae aliquo moda, aliqua causa, aliqua parte mutabilis est: Deum autem nefas est, nisi veré summeque incommutabilem credere. Non est igitur anima pars Dei» (Epist. 166 c.2 n.3: ML 33,721). The basic principle of its refutation is clearly metaphysical. He formulates it in De anima et eius origine (1.1 c.19 n.32): "Nam de quo quisque naturae suae originem dur.it, de illa naturae suae genus ducere negari sobrie nullo Pacto Potesl." Without dwelling on other attributes, he focuses on the changes to which the soul is subject, while God is immutable by essence: "Therefore, it does not part of the substance of God." 2. Anima-spiritus.—It is not easy to rigorously specify the Augustinian meaning of these two words. It is necessary to go to the context in each case. In general terms it can be said that the soul is the life-giving principle of the body. Thus, man and animal have souls (cf. A. MARTIN, Sancti Aurelii Augustini Philosophia [Paris 1863] p.351). Spirituality is used in two different meanings. When used in the sense derived from Porphyry (cf. De civ. Dei 1.10 c.9 n.2: ML 12, 286), it designates "a coordinating principle of bodily images." It belongs to the second degree, being superior to the vital principle (anima) and inferior to understanding (mens), something similar to what scholastics call imagination or sensitive memory (cf. De Gen. ad litt. p.12 c.24 n.51: ML 34,474; E. GILSON, introduction á tetude de Saint Augustin p.55 note 1). Taken in the biblical meaning, spiritus is equivalent to "spirit" or "mind" (cf. De anima et eius origine 1.4 c.22 n.36; E. GILSON, l. c). In this sense, the "spirit" is typical of man: it is the faculty with which "ratiocinamur, intelligimus, sapimus" (De anima et eius origine l.c). The spirit is not something different from the soul, but "aliquid in anima" (ibid.). 3. Foreknowledge and causality.—Vincent Victor spoke of God's foreknowledge in relation to the fall of souls, according to his hypothesis of preexistence (cf. De anima et eius origine 1.1 c.7 n.7; c.9 n.15; 1.2 c.9 n.15).

Saint Augustine responds with a very clear distinction: God's foreknowledge is the foresight and not the cause of evil: "Praescientia quippe Dei... peccatores praenoscit, non facit." 4. Paradise and the kingdom of heaven.—Vincent Victor pointed out a place of happiness that he called “paradise,” where the souls of children who died without baptism and those who passed from this life without having received it and without serious personal sins temporarily remained. After the resurrection they would also enter the kingdom of heaven (cf. De anima et eius origine 1.1 c.9 n.10; 1.2 c.12 n.16; 1.3 c.ll n.15.16.17 and 19). Saint Augustine does not allow this distinction and identifies paradise with the kingdom of heaven, into which nothing defiled will enter.

5. The Censor.—"Give him the honors of a censor, if those of a doctor are not enough" (De anima et eius origine 1.2 c.ll n.15). The irony of Saint Augustine is visible. The censors were established in Rome in the year 311 of the Republic (443 BC). In the time of the Saint, the mission of that magistracy extended to the surveillance of customs, morals, law and matters pertinent to the cult and care of the temples. As Vicente Victor judged that the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ should be offered even by those who had not been incorporated into it, Saint Augustine applied the title of censor to him. 6. The inner man.—Victor giving an inaccurate interpretation to some words of Saint Paul to the Thessalonians (1 c.6 v.23), he distinguished three substances in man: the soul or the inner man, the spirit or the intimate man, the body or the external man (De anima et eius origine 1.4 c.14 n.20). Saint Augustine makes him see and demonstrates the inappropriateness of such a distinction; for the Apostle speaks only of the inner man and the outer man. The inner man is the soul and everything that refers to the soul or spirit. INTRODUCTION

The brief treatise On the Nature of Good belongs to the series of works that Saint Augustine dedicated to combating and refuting the errors of Manichaeism. It is known that he entered the sect seeking the truth, which the disciples of Manes shouted and preached at all hours and everywhere. Great was his neophyte enthusiasm for the Manichean doctrines; But his interest was greater, after his conversion, in undeceiving the unfortunate people caught in the same networks of error into which he had fallen. His position guaranteed success. To the acuity of his dialectic and his wit was added the circumstance of thoroughly knowing the internal and external, the doctrinal and the ritual of Manichaeism. Much of his literary production is dedicated to this object. It can be said that the controversy lasted from his conversion until his death, since it began with the treatise On the Customs of the Catholic Church and the Customs of the Manichaeans (387-388) and ended with Chapter XLVI of the book On Heresies (428). The dogmatic basis of Manichaeism is dualism, consisting of the admission of two opposite and equally eternal principles: Good and Evil: of two natures made up of contrary principles, one being intrinsically good and the other essentially bad, and of two kingdoms, that of Light and that of Darkness, which correspond to the two principles. Between these two kingdoms there was a long period of peace, due to the ignorance of the world of Darkness in relation to that of Light. When the inhabitants of that city became aware of the admirable and charming spectacle that the kingdom of Light presented, they agreed to assault it and mix with them. Such was the origin of the fight between the princes of the two kingdoms. During the battle, many particles of light were confused or mixed with those of the nature of evil, becoming imprisoned in matter. These particles must be freed so that they do not suffer the condemnation to which matter is subject. Its liberation is carried out daily throughout the world and in its elements, and in a special way it is verified by the elect through food and drink, acts by which the particles of light, freed from the bonds of darkness, are transported to the kingdom of God in two luminous ships, which are the moon and the sun. Saint Augustine himself notes this fact as one of the driving reasons for his registration in Manichaeism. Cf. Confess. 1.3 n.6 n.

The exposition of these concepts, or better, of these fables, as Saint Augustine qualifies them, constitutes the background of the treatise On the Nature of Good, composed at the beginning of the year 405, and of the remaining polemical works against the Manichaeans. The Augustinian P. F. Cayré believes that the first is the one that best summarizes the anti-Manichean doctrine of Saint Augustine 3. In the book On the Nature of Good we can see two clearly differentiated parts. Saint Augustine first expounds the timeless principles on the philosophy of good and evil (c.1-39), and then goes on to directly refute what he calls impious blasphemies, with which the Manichaeans attribute the most heinous follies to the nature of God (c.40-48). As A. Gardeil and E. Masson observe, it was Saint Augustine who was the first to give a complete philosophy on the nature and origin of good and evil. In this work he develops these problems in almost all their aspects 4. Regarding the good, many of the Anguslinian formulas recall expressions from some of Plato's dialogues, for example, the Philebus, or pleasure, and the Theaetetus, or science, contained in Neoplatonic philosophy. Later Saint Thomas Aquinas used them and frequently quotes them in his works. The general argument or thesis can be reduced to these points: a) God is the supreme being and the supreme good; b) everything created, material or immaterial, comes from God; c) the goodness of creatures consists in the manner, in the beauty and in the order: modus, species el ordo. Once these foundations are established, it is easy to answer the insistent question of the Manichaeans: "Where does evil come from?" To respond appropriately it is necessary to first know what evil is, that is, its nature. The Manichaeans considered it as a separate substance, a substantial principle different from the good. Saint Augustine approaches the question from a metaphysical point of view, to reach the conclusion that evil is the corruption of good, and it is not possible to conceive or suppose the existence of an absolutely evil principle. In the last chapters he exposes the abominations of Manichean beliefs and practices, highlighting the outrage they infer to the nature of God. 1. Deus, summum Bonum (el).—Saint Augustine accepts this terminology of Platonic origin to proclaim the sovereignty or excellency of God, inasmuch as he is the first cause and the first principle of all created beings. 2. Modus, species, ordo (c.3).—E. Gilson and P. V. Capánaga see in these expressions a vestige of the Trinity, on which the latter says the goodness of the universe rests or rests. These three general goods are the foundation of Augustinian ontology (ci. E. GILSON, Introduction a Vétude de Saint Augustin p.282 note 2; P. V. CAPÁNAGA, A. R., Obras de San Agustín: General Introduction [BAC, Madrid 1946] vol.l p.41). 3. The harmony of creation (c.7.8.9.27).—Perfect is the hierarchy in the scale of beings, subordinated from inferior to superior or most excellent. The formation is so ordered that even punishments contribute to reestablishing the harmony broken by sin, God bringing good out of evil and making sinners reintegrate into the universal order they have transfixed (cf. G. PHILIPS, La raison d'étre du mal d'aprés Saint Augustin [Lovain 1927] p.108-115). 4. liylé or matter (c.18).—With this name Manes designated the principle of evil, an essentially evil substance, which he considered the formator or creator of all bodies. A bad substance is something contradictory. If good and being are confused, evil cannot have its own entity. But Saint Augustine is not referring in this passage to matter understood according to the Manichean system, but to the concept that the ancient philosophers formed of it: to raw matter in the Aristotelian sense, capable of receiving visible forms: "Habet enim et ipsa capamatem formarum." Taking into account the context, it does not seem that the word formosi can be translated simply as "beautiful." It would have this meaning if it were contrasted with "deformed", as King Al tuna contrasts them: formosusdeformis (cf. What is the beautiful. Introduction to the Aesthetics of Saint Augustine p.52). But in this chapter Saint Augustine focuses on analyzing the raw material, and writes: "Hylen dico quamdam penitus informam et sine qualitate materiem, unde istae quas sentimus qualitates formatur, ut antiqui dixerunt." Report is, therefore, that which lacks form. When beings have it, they are called formed. 5. Being by essence (c.19).—The definition of Divinity given by itself serves Saint Augustine to point out the essential difference between the Creator and the creatures.

He is the immutable, while creatures are subject to mutability, that is, to ceasing to be what they were, because they do not have being by essence: "quia nihil est unde factae sunt" (c.10). 6. Evil, privation of good (c.4.16.23).—This is the conclusion reached by Saint Augustine after analyzing the origin of beings. In the Confessions he speaks of "deprivation of good" to explain the nature of evil (1.12 c.7 n.12: PL 32,688). In the treatise De natura boni he calls evil "corruption of manner, or beauty, or order." In the City of God he repeats this same thought: "Non est causa efficiens, sed deficiens, quia malum non est effectio, sed defectio" (1.12 c.7: PL

41,357). This phrase of Saint Augustine has given rise to the well-known axiom: "Malum habet causam non efficientem, sed deficiencym." This deprivation may have as its object a physical good or a moral good. In the first case it is a consequence of the imperfection of the creature, which comes from nothing and tends to cease to be (c.10). In the second case, deprivation comes from the free will of man, from a deviation of the will, which gives preference to an inferior good over a more excellent one (c.34). 7. Chosen listeners (c.44).—The external rigor of Manichean morality was superior to the strength of most men. That is why there were two categories among them: the elect and the listeners. The former had the obligation to observe all the precepts. The listeners belonged to a lower grade and formed the mass, the people. Saint Augustine did not go beyond a simple listener in the nine years that he remained in the Manichean sect.
